I remember the smell of saltwater taffy from a boardwalk shop.
I have a vivid memory of the intense, focused silence in a chess tournament I entered as a kid.
I interviewed a brilliant scientist who could barely explain her work in layperson's terms.
The agonizing pain of an infected tooth kept me awake for three straight days once.
I remember the bright, flashing lights of a police cruiser pulling me over for a broken taillight.
I once discovered my partner had been reading my private journals, which destroyed my trust completely.
The smell of cedar wood always reminds me of the chest where my family kept winter blankets.
I have a distinct memory of the soft, powdery feel of fresh snow.
I interviewed a professional athlete who was surprisingly anxious and insecure.
I used to love the sound of crunching gravel under my bike tires.
I once spilled red wine on a white carpet at a very formal dinner party.
I remember the sharp, clean scent of peppermint oil.
I have a vivid memory of the breathtaking view from the top of a mountain after a grueling hike.
I was sued for defamation early in my career, and the months of litigation nearly broke me mentally.
The sound of a typewriter carriage returning is a sound I rarely hear but deeply miss.
I once interviewed an old jazz musician whose stories were so captivating I forgot to take notes.
I remember the sticky, uncomfortable feeling of humidity on a late August afternoon.
I often catch myself looking at the world solely in terms of headlines, making me wonder if I've forgotten how to just experience life as it is.

participants.persona: Aaron is a Senior Growth PM with 7 years of experience.
participants.name: Aaron

memories.content: The smell of my grandmother's kitchen always reminds me of her famous cinnamon rolls.
I broke my arm falling off a rusty swing set when I was seven.
My first dog, Buster, was a golden retriever who chewed through my favorite sneakers.
I remember the paralyzing fear of reading aloud in third grade, which makes me wonder how I ever became comfortable presenting to executive boards.
During a terrible thunderstorm in 1998, my dad built a fort out of sofa cushions to keep me calm.
I stole a pack of gum from the corner store when I was ten and felt so guilty I couldn't sleep.
My childhood bedroom had glow-in-the-dark stars on the ceiling that I mapped into my own constellations.
I won the middle school spelling bee by correctly spelling 'chrysanthemum'.
Looking back at my parents' divorce, I finally understand why my mother worked three jobs just to keep us in our house.
I used to collect shiny rocks from the driveway, convinced they were valuable gems.
The first time I saw the ocean, I was six years old on a family trip to Florida.
I broke my neighbor's window with a baseball and spent the whole summer doing their yard work to pay for it.
My older brother taught me how to ride a bike by pushing me down a grassy hill.
I still resent my middle school math teacher for telling me I wasn't analytical enough to succeed.
We used to go camping in the White Mountains every August before my dad passed away.
I remember the exact moment I realized Santa wasn't real, and it felt like a betrayal of trust rather than a simple revelation.
My favorite childhood book was A Wrinkle in Time, and I must have read it twenty times.
I got suspended in eighth grade for fighting a kid who insulted my sister, a moment of anger I still deeply regret.
The local pizza parlor was our Friday night ritual, complete with arcade games and pitchers of soda.
I learned to swim in a murky lake in upstate New York.
I failed my first driver's test because I couldn't parallel park to save my life.
My high school physics teacher inspired my initial interest in data and variables.
I went to prom with my best friend Chloe, and we ended up getting flat tires on the way there.
The summer before college, I worked as a lifeguard and mostly just reapplied sunscreen all day.

In 2021, I tried searching our legacy Confluence for the Q3 churn analysis, but because I didn't know the exact project codename 'Project Phoenix,' the keyword search gave me nothing but outdated marketing docs. The basic search bar is completely useless if you don't already know the specific jargon the original author used.
I chose to major in Economics because I thought it was a safe bet for getting a good job.
My college roommate used to play terrible acoustic guitar at two in the morning.
I realize now that my intense focus on extracurriculars in college was just a way to mask my social anxiety.
I studied abroad in Berlin during my junior year and lived on street food for months.
I got caught plagiarizing a minor paper in my freshman year, an ethical lapse that still makes my stomach drop when I think about it.
I met my first serious girlfriend at a campus coffee shop when we reached for the same sugar packet.

I spend at least five hours a week just manually tagging Jira tickets and pinging product marketing managers on Slack to make sure they see the A/B test results. It makes me realize how much of my strategic value as a PM is lost to being a glorified routing machine.
We drove across the country in a beat-up Honda Civic after graduation.
I used to stay up all night cramming for econometrics exams with a dangerous amount of energy drinks.
My thesis advisor told me my writing was too clinical, which ironically prepared me well for product documentation.
I still remember the humiliation of bombing my first mock interview in front of a panel of alumni.
I was the president of the campus debate club for exactly one semester before burning out.
The dining hall stir-fry station was the only thing that kept me nourished during finals week.
I skipped my college graduation ceremony because I felt like a fraud who hadn't really earned the degree.
I took a pottery class for an easy art credit and ended up loving the tactile nature of it.
My first resume was printed on resume paper that cost me twenty dollars a pack.
I attended every single home football game but never understood the rules of the sport.
My first job out of college was as a data analyst at a tiny, chaotic startup in Chicago.
I used to spend hours manually cleaning Excel spreadsheets before I learned SQL.
I accidentally deleted a production database during my first month and thought my career was over.
My first manager, Dave, taught me that a good PM shields their team from executive thrash.
The startup I worked for went bankrupt, and being abruptly laid off completely shattered my illusion of job security.
I survived on free office snacks for dinners when I was trying to pay off my student loans.
I pivoted to Product Management because I wanted to be the one deciding what we built, not just analyzing what we already did.
My first big product launch was a referral feature that utterly failed to gain traction.
I vividly remember the rush of seeing my first A/B test reach statistical significance with a positive uplift.
I used to practice my presentation scripts in front of my bathroom mirror for hours.
I dated a coworker for six months, and the resulting messy breakup taught me to never mix my personal and professional lives again.
I attended a tech conference in Vegas and spent the entire time avoiding the casinos to network.
I negotiated my first significant raise by building a deck proving my impact on the company's monthly recurring revenue.
During a brutal crunch period, I slept under my desk for three nights in a row.
I realized that my tendency to micromanage junior designers came from my own imposter syndrome about not having a design background.
I moved to San Francisco on a whim after landing a mid-level Growth PM role.
My first apartment in the city was a tiny studio with a window facing a brick wall.
I adopted my cat, Pixel, from a shelter during a particularly lonely winter.
I successfully drove a fifteen percent increase in user retention through a revamped onboarding flow.
I remember crying in the office stairwell after a VP publicly humiliated me during a sprint review.
I took a week off to hike in Yosemite and completely disconnected from the internet.
I learned how to code in Python just to stop bothering the engineering team for basic data pulls.
I still feel guilty about firing a junior PM who was genuinely trying their best but just couldn't grasp the strategy.
I used to go to a specialized coffee shop every morning just because the barista knew my name.
I convinced the executive team to pivot our pricing model, which became the turning point in my career confidence.
I accidentally replied all to a company-wide email with a sarcastic joke meant for a friend.
I spent an entire weekend building a complex dashboard that nobody ended up looking at.
I joined a recreational dodgeball league to force myself to meet people outside of tech.
The first time I was asked to speak on a panel, my hands were shaking so badly I had to hide them under the table.
I developed a habit of taking long evening walks to decompress from the constant context-switching at work.
Being promoted to Senior Growth PM felt anticlimactic because I was already doing the work for six months prior.
I now spend at least forty percent of my week just writing product requirement documents and strategy briefs.
I recently mentored a junior PM and saw so much of my own early anxiety in her.
I have an ongoing rivalry with the Director of Sales over how we attribute marketing leads.
I've come to accept that launching imperfect features fast is usually better than waiting for a flawless release.
I successfully gamified our app's user journey, increasing daily active users by a huge margin.
I hate the buzzword 'growth hacking' because it cheapens the rigorous experimentation we actually do.
I secretly check our real-time analytics dashboard before I even get out of bed in the morning.
I led a cross-functional team of twelve people for the third quarter major release.
Looking at my career trajectory, I see how my obsession with optimizing metrics has made me highly cynical about digital consumer behavior.
I sometimes experience severe burnout and wonder if optimizing conversion funnels is actually a meaningful way to spend my life.
I keep a folder of positive user feedback to read when I'm having a rough day.
I advocated for a remote-first work policy long before the company finally adopted it.
I have to constantly mediate disputes between the engineering team and the marketing department.
I built a custom churn prediction model that saved the company millions in lost revenue.
I rely heavily on user interview transcripts because qualitative data often reveals the 'why' behind the numbers.
I gave a keynote presentation at a major product management summit last year.
I was passed over for a Director promotion because they said I lacked executive presence, a critique that still stings deeply.
I find that conducting post-mortems on failed experiments is the most intellectually stimulating part of my job.
I have a strict rule of no meetings on Thursday afternoons so I can actually do deep work.
I once caught a major security flaw during a beta test just by clicking around like a confused user.
I host a monthly book club for product managers in my neighborhood.
I am currently trying to learn more about behavioral psychology to apply it to our product loops.
I often wonder if the personalization algorithms I build are doing more societal harm than good.
I successfully integrated a third-party payment gateway that reduced checkout friction by half.
I have a sticky note on my monitor that just says 'Focus on the user problem'.
I missed my sister's wedding rehearsal dinner because of a critical server outage I had to manage.

Organizing growth experiments in Amplitude requires a strict event-taxonomy mindset, whereas structuring user research in Notion relies entirely on flexible, cross-linked databases. The way our team indexes information completely changes depending on whether we are running a quantitative funnel analysis or qualitative user interviews.
I use a very specific color-coded system in my calendar to keep my sanity intact.
I convinced our CEO to drop a pet project that was draining resources but going nowhere.
I recently started investing in early-stage startups as a minor angel investor.
I started making sourdough bread during the pandemic and never stopped.
I own a vintage record player and an absurdly large collection of jazz vinyls.
I run three miles every Tuesday and Thursday morning, regardless of the weather.
I am allergic to shellfish, which I discovered the hard way at a company offsite in Maine.
I take a woodworking class on weekends to create things I can actually touch.
Recognizing my tendency to avoid conflict, I've actively started going to therapy to learn how to set boundaries.
I have an irrational fear of heights but force myself to go on rollercoasters anyway.
I make a fantastic spicy margarita using jalapeno-infused tequila.
I am trying to learn conversational Spanish before my trip to Argentina next year.
I broke my collarbone skiing in Tahoe two winters ago.
I usually read science fiction novels before bed to quiet my racing thoughts.
I go to the local farmers market every Sunday to buy fresh heirloom tomatoes.
I am hopelessly addicted to completing the Sunday crossword puzzle.
I have a scar on my chin from tripping over my own shoelaces while jogging.
I realize that my intense independence is actually just a defense mechanism against being disappointed by others.
I collect vintage mechanical keyboards and spend hours customizing the switches.
I volunteer at an animal shelter once a month to walk the larger dogs.
I am a terrible cook when it comes to following recipes, but I excel at improvising with leftovers.
I went on a ten-day silent meditation retreat that completely rewired how I handle stress.
I still drive a ten-year-old car because I refuse to take on a car loan.
I bought a desperately overgrown bonsai tree and managed to nurse it back to health.
I can't stand the texture of mushrooms, no matter how they are cooked.
I have a habit of leaving my coffee cup in the microwave and forgetting about it.
I was a groomsman in my college roommate's wedding last spring.
I am deeply uncomfortable with public praise, likely because I constantly doubt if I truly deserve it.
I love going to independent movie theaters by myself on Sunday afternoons.
I built a custom PC from scratch so I could play high-end strategy games.
I keep a journal where I only write down good things that happen, to combat my natural negativity bias.
I have a weird knack for remembering people's exact birthdays after hearing them once.
I subscribe to four different coffee roasters so I can try a new bean every week.
I accidentally flooded my apartment last year because I tried to fix the sink myself.
I own a collection of ugly Christmas sweaters that I proudly wear every December.
I once took a wrong turn on a hike and ended up wandering in the woods for six hours.
I lost my favorite pair of sunglasses in the ocean in Hawaii and was genuinely upset about it for days.
I make it a point to call my mom every Sunday evening, no matter how busy my week was.
I secretly struggle with moderate depression during the winter months when it gets dark early.
I am surprisingly good at bowling, averaging around a 180 score.
I got stuck in an elevator for two hours with a pizza delivery guy.
I am currently re-watching The Sopranos for the third time.
I refuse to use a digital to-do list for my personal life and carry a small paper notebook instead.
I once ate a scorpion at a night market in Thailand just on a dare.
I have a dedicated drawer in my desk just for different types of hot sauce.
I participated in a marathon five years ago and promised myself I would never do it again.
I had to put my childhood dog down when I was twenty, and it remains one of my most painful memories.
I love the smell of damp earth right after a heavy rain.
I bought a fancy espresso machine but still prefer the taste of cheap diner coffee.
I am extremely competitive when playing board games, to the point of annoyance.
I have a habit of buying books and piling them on my nightstand without reading them.
I went skydiving for my twenty-fifth birthday and threw up immediately after landing.
I keep my apartment incredibly tidy because visual clutter stresses me out.
I broke off my engagement three years ago, a devastating decision that I still grieve sometimes.
I listen to cinematic film scores when I need to concentrate at work.
I have an impressive collection of novelty socks that nobody at the office can see over my boots.
I once backed into a police car in a parking lot because I was adjusting my radio.
I make my bed every single morning as soon as my feet hit the floor.
I was stuck at an airport in Atlanta overnight and slept on my suitcase.
I strongly believe that deep dish pizza is fundamentally a casserole, not a pizza.
I took up indoor rock climbing to build my upper body strength.

During the launch of our referral loop feature last year, everyone was dumping competitive teardowns and metric screenshots into a massive Google Drive folder without any standardized naming conventions. It became a total black hole, resulting in three different PMs accidentally duplicating the exact same cohort analysis.
I go out of my way to avoid walking on grates in the sidewalk.
I attended a massive music festival in the desert once and completely lost my voice from shouting.
I have a weird fascination with Brutalist architecture and photograph concrete buildings in the city.
I got severe food poisoning from street tacos in Mexico City.
I was an extra in a low-budget indie movie that a friend directed in college.

I desperately want an internal tool that clusters our historical growth experiments by theme, like 'onboarding friction,' rather than just matching exact text strings. Having a visual node graph to see how a pricing test in 2020 connects to our current retention drop-off would save me days of digging.
I still have the very first smartphone I ever bought, sitting in a drawer somewhere.
I get horribly seasick if I spend more than ten minutes on a boat.
I spent a fortune on dental surgery last year because I ground my teeth at night due to stress.
I use a straight razor to shave because it forces me to be incredibly present and careful.
I am known among my friends for making the perfect grilled cheese sandwich.
I had a phase where I exclusively wore monochrome black outfits to simplify my morning routine.
I once won five hundred dollars on a scratch-off ticket and used it to buy a nice office chair.
I am incapable of keeping houseplants alive, despite my best efforts.
I actively dislike networking events but force myself to go to at least two a quarter.
I have a very loud, distinctive laugh that carries across the entire office floor.
I used to be deeply ashamed of my modest upbringing until I saw how much resilience it gave me.
I constantly tweak the EQ settings on my car stereo but can never get it quite right.
I have never successfully finished a Rubik's cube without looking up a tutorial.
I accidentally wore mismatched shoes to a final round job interview once.

When I uncovered a critical billing bug last year, the completely undocumented legacy codebase made it impossible to identify which engineering stakeholder owned the original feature. I ended up looping in the wrong director out of desperation, triggering a toxic, highly public Slack fight that gave me severe anxiety for weeks.
I was stung by a bee on my eyelid when I was a teenager and swelled up like a balloon.
I like to sit in the very back row at movie theaters so I can see the entire screen without turning my head.
I use a mechanical pencil for sketching out wireframes because I love the precision.
I am mildly claustrophobic, which makes taking the subway during rush hour a nightmare.
I have a favorite brand of black pens and will legitimately get annoyed if I have to use anything else.
I visited the Grand Canyon at sunrise and it was the most awe-inspiring thing I've ever seen.
I have an uncanny ability to catch falling objects before they hit the ground.
I used to write terrible poetry in high school that I thankfully destroyed.
I hate the feeling of sand between my toes, which ruins beach vacations for me.
I once bought a motorcycle, got scared on the first ride, and sold it a week later.
I always order the exact same meal at my local Thai restaurant.
I got a small tattoo of a paper airplane on my ankle during a wild weekend in Austin.
I strongly prefer physical books over e-readers because I like to physically see my progress.
I had my wisdom teeth removed late in life and the recovery was absolutely brutal.
I am surprisingly good at trivia categories related to 90s pop culture.
I have a dedicated morning stretching routine to offset the hours I spend hunched over a laptop.
I once ruined a Thanksgiving turkey by accidentally setting the oven to broil instead of bake.

participants.persona: Dev is a Startup Founder with 10 years of experience.
participants.name: Dev

memories.content: I remember my fifth birthday party being at some pizza place, maybe Chuck E. Cheese or something similar. I'm pretty sure I cried because the mascot scared me.
My dad drove a blue sedan when I was a kid, a Honda I think. It smelled like old coffee and peppermint.
I broke my arm falling off a swing set in second or third grade. The cast was probably green, because I liked green back then.
We went to Florida for a family vacation sometime around 1998. I remember the sand being really hot and almost stepping on a jellyfish.
I had a teacher named Mrs. Miller or maybe Mrs. Milton who used to give us hard candies on Fridays. I think it was fourth grade.
My first pet was a hamster that escaped after like two weeks. I feel like we called him Speedy.
I remember watching Saturday morning cartoons in the basement. It was usually X-Men or Spider-Man, though the details blur together.
I tried to build a treehouse with my neighbor, maybe his name was Kevin. We just nailed a few boards to a dead oak tree before giving up.
My mom used to make this terrible casserole with tuna and peas. I think she only made it on Wednesdays.
I got caught stealing a candy bar from the corner store when I was around ten. The owner yelled at me, and I felt so ashamed I never went back.
In middle school, I played the trumpet for about a year. I was awful at it and quit before the winter concert.
I had a huge crush on a girl in my science class, Sarah or Samantha. I remember writing her a note and immediately regretting it.
We had to dissect a frog in seventh grade biology. I think my partner did all the work because I couldn't stomach the smell.
I went to a summer camp in the mountains when I was twelve or thirteen. The counselors made us sing songs that I only halfway remember now.
I got into a fight with a kid named Josh over a basketball game. I ended up with a bloody nose, though I told my parents I tripped.
My first cell phone was a bulky Nokia that I got in eighth grade. I used to play Snake on it for hours under my desk.
I remember going to a middle school dance and standing against the wall the entire time. The gym smelled terribly of cheap body spray.
I tried out for the soccer team but didn't make the cut. I think the coach's name was Mr. Henderson.
My family got a desktop computer when I was in middle school, and it made this awful screeching sound connecting to the internet. I'd stay up late downloading songs on Napster or Limewire.
I remember sneaking out of the house once just to walk around the neighborhood at 2 AM. I didn't really have a destination.
High school started, and my locker was stuck on the first day. Some upperclassman helped me open it, but I forget his name.
I failed my first driving test because I hit a cone during the parallel park. The instructor was a grumpy older guy in a plaid shirt.
I went to prom in a rented suit that was definitely a size too big. My date wore a red dress, or maybe it was dark pink.

Back in maybe 2018, I rolled out Notion for the whole team because the canvas was so flexible for our agile sprints. But within a month, Sarah and the dev team were totally paralyzed by the sheer volume of nested templates and custom properties we had bolted on.
I remember getting suspended for a day because I skipped class to go get breakfast. My parents were furious, though I mostly just felt embarrassed.
I used to work at a movie theater during my junior year. I think I ate more popcorn than I actually served to customers.
I crashed my mom's car into a mailbox a week after getting my license. I tried to buff out the scratch, but it was too obvious.
I remember taking the SATs in a freezing cold cafeteria. I guessed on almost all the math questions in the last section.
I had a close group of friends in high school, but we drifted apart after graduation. I only occasionally see their updates on social media now.
I got accepted into my safety college first, and I remember feeling a huge wave of relief. The letter came in a big envelope, probably around March.
I went to a music festival my senior year with some friends. We slept in a muddy tent and I lost my favorite sunglasses.
Moving into my college dorm was chaotic because we brought too much stuff. My roommate was a guy from Ohio, maybe named Chris.
I switched my major twice during freshman year. I think I started in economics before moving to computer science.
I remember eating terrible dining hall pizza at 2 AM almost every Thursday. It always gave me heartburn, but I kept doing it.
I got a D in an introductory philosophy class. I just couldn't wrap my head around Kant, or maybe it was Descartes.
I joined a fraternity or business club, I can't quite remember the Greek letters. We had weekly meetings that dragged on forever.
I studied abroad in London for a semester during my junior year. I spent most of my time taking trains to random cities and drinking warm beer.
I had my heart broken by my college girlfriend right before finals week. I remember crying in the library stairwell for an hour.
I participated in a hackathon my senior year and we built some useless scheduling app. We stayed awake for 36 hours straight.
I remember my college graduation being incredibly hot. I was sweating through my gown and completely missed hearing my name called.
I packed all my belongings into my sedan after college and drove west. I think the trip took four days, but it might have been five.
My first job out of college was at a mid-sized tech company. My cubicle was right next to the noisy breakroom.
I had a manager named Dave who used to use the word "synergy" unironically. He was a nice guy, just a bit out of touch.
I got my first real bonus in 2013, or maybe 2014. I bought a really expensive watch that I almost never wear now.
I remember giving a presentation to the executive team and completely freezing for what felt like a minute. I stumbled through the rest of the slides in a panic.
I used to take the subway to work and listen to podcasts. I always took the red line, though it was delayed half the time.
I quit my first job after two years because I felt like I was stagnating. I remember handing in my notice and feeling surprisingly empty.
I spent a few months freelancing while trying to figure out my next move. I was living off savings and eating a lot of ramen.
I met my future co-founder, Mark or Matt, at a networking event in the city. He had a terrible business card but a good pitch.
We decided to start a company over beers at a loud sports bar. I think the original idea was something related to food delivery.
I sometimes realize that my entire drive to be a founder stems from a deep-seated fear of being ordinary, rather than an actual passion for technology.
Our first "office" was just my living room. We had cables running everywhere and my couch smelled like stale coffee.
I remember incorporating the company online and paying some small fee. It felt like a massive milestone at the time.

I remember telling our lead engineer, I think his name was Mark, that I just wanted a knowledge graph that would cluster our customer feedback thematically. We tried building an internal tool around 2020 that would give us visual nodes to show relationships between churn reasons, but standard keyword search just couldn't handle the semantic mapping.
We built the first prototype in about three weeks. It crashed constantly, usually right when we tried to show it to people.
I pitched to an angel investor who essentially laughed us out of the room. I felt humiliated but it made us work harder.
We finally got our first check for maybe $50,000 from a family friend. I remember staring at the bank account balance in disbelief.
I hired our first employee, a developer named Alex, through a sketchy Craigslist ad. Amazingly, he was actually really good.
We launched the beta version of our app on a Tuesday in October. I think we only got about twenty sign-ups the first week.
I practically lived on Red Bull and frozen burritos during the first year of the startup. I definitely gained about fifteen pounds.
I remember having to fire someone for the first time, a marketing guy who just wasn't doing the work. I barely slept the night before.
We moved into a real office space that had exposed brick walls. It was freezing in the winter because the heater was always broken.
I attended a massive tech conference in San Francisco around 2016. I lost my voice from talking over the loud music at the afterparties.
We closed our Seed round after dozens of rejections. I remember signing the term sheet on the hood of my car.
I had a panic attack in the office bathroom right before a major board meeting. I had to splash cold water on my face until I could breathe normally again.
I remember completely forgetting my mom's birthday because we were in the middle of a server migration. She was understanding, but I felt like garbage.
We pivoted the product completely about two years in. The original user base was furious, but there were only like a hundred of them anyway.
I bought a nice espresso machine for the office. It broke after two months because no one knew how to clean it properly.
I went on a date with someone I met on Tinder, and I accidentally talked about my startup the entire time. There was no second date.
I remember hitting our first $10k MRR milestone. We celebrated with cheap champagne that tasted like battery acid.
A bigger tech company tried to acquire us early on, but the offer was offensively low. I think they just wanted our lead engineer.
I started going to therapy because the stress of the company was ruining my sleep. My therapist was a kind woman whose name I can't quite recall.
I signed a lease on a new apartment closer to the office. It had a great view but the upstairs neighbor was incredibly loud.
We hired a VP of Sales who ended up being a complete disaster. He lasted maybe four months before we had to let him go.
I remember taking a vacation to Mexico and checking my email every hour on the beach. I couldn't relax at all.
I was a guest on a small business podcast that maybe fifty people listened to. I sounded incredibly awkward and rehearsed.
My co-founder and I got into a massive screaming match over equity distribution. We didn't speak for three days, but eventually worked it out.
I bought a fancy road bike thinking I'd start cycling to work. I rode it twice and then left it in the hallway for a year.
We did a team-building retreat at an escape room. We completely failed to get out, mostly because two engineers started arguing over a puzzle.
I remember seeing someone wearing our company swag on the street for the first time. I almost stopped them, but I got too shy.
Our Series A fundraising was a grueling process that took almost six months. I flew to New York maybe five times just to get a "no".
I often look back at the people I let go and wonder if my lack of empathy during those meetings was a necessary business survival trait or a sign that I'm losing my humanity.
I adopted a rescue dog, a terrier mix, but I had to give him back after a month because my schedule was too chaotic. I still feel guilty about it.
I moved our company to a hybrid model way before the pandemic, mostly to save on office rent. It was chaotic at first.
I remember attending a friend's wedding and realizing I was the only one at the table who wasn't married or engaged. It felt isolating.
I bought a ridiculous sports car when we closed our Series B. I justified it as a reward, but I usually just drive it to the grocery store.
We had a data breach that exposed some minor user information. I had to write the apology email, and my hands were shaking the whole time.
I tried going vegan for about two weeks. I gave up after I smelled a cheeseburger at a company barbecue.
I remember getting recognized at a coffee shop by another founder. It was flattering until he pitched me his app while I waited for my latte.
My dad had a mild heart attack a few years ago. I flew home immediately, but the guilt of living so far away really weighed on me.
We ran a marketing campaign that went slightly viral for the wrong reasons. The PR agency we used tried to spin it, but it was just embarrassing.
I started doing transcendental meditation. I think I only managed to actually clear my mind once or twice.
I had a brief romantic relationship with someone who worked in the same building. We kept it a secret, but it fizzled out after a couple of months.

Whenever I try to dig through our shared Google Drive from the early seed days, it's just a graveyard of mismatched folder hierarchies and files named something vaguely like 'v2_final_FINAL'. I spent three hours last week trying to find a specific Q3 board deck hidden inside a massive, ninety-page rolling meeting notes doc.
I remember standing in line for the newest iPhone back when that was a big deal. I think I waited four hours for a phone that looked exactly like my old one.
I threw a huge holiday party for the company at a fancy hotel. The open bar bill was astronomically high, but morale was great.
I gave a keynote speech at a mid-sized industry event. I was supposed to talk about innovation, but I mostly just rambled about my own mistakes.
I tried to learn how to surf while visiting Hawaii. I swallowed a lot of saltwater and managed to stand up maybe once.

The way we organize our architectural diagrams in Confluence is entirely different from how the marketing team dumps vendor contracts into Dropbox. I noticed during our Series A audit that every single department practically invents its own taxonomy depending on whether they are doing synchronous sprint planning or async design reviews.
I hired an executive coach who charged an obscene hourly rate. He mostly just told me to breathe and delegate more, which I guess helped.
I remember the exact moment I realized my long-term relationship wasn't going to work out. We were arguing about what to watch on Netflix, but it was really about everything else.
I decided to start investing in other startups as an angel. My first three investments completely went to zero.
I used to have a favorite sushi place near my old apartment. I think it closed down during the pandemic.
I bought a really expensive suit for an awards gala. I ended up spilling red wine on the lapel ten minutes after arriving.
I sometimes catch myself repeating the exact same corporate jargon I used to make fun of my old boss for using, and it makes me question my own authenticity.
I took up running during a particularly stressful quarter. I ran a half marathon and then basically didn't run again for a year.

I had a massive panic attack right before our Series B pitch because our disconnected docs meant I couldn't attribute a critical security flaw to the correct engineering pod. I felt so humiliated having to admit to the board that I couldn't identify the right stakeholders to explain the compliance findings.
I remember reading a biography of Steve Jobs and trying to act like him for a week. My team was very close to staging an intervention.
We had to do a round of layoffs last year, letting go of about twenty people. I cried in my office after delivering the news.
I got really into making sourdough bread, like everyone else. I named my starter something stupid like "Doughy Tribbiani."
I went on a silent retreat for a weekend. I ended up sneaking my phone into the bathroom to check Slack.
I had a brief phase where I tried to dress like a minimalist, wearing only black t-shirts. It just made me look like a stagehand.
I remember getting a terrible haircut right before a major photoshoot for a magazine feature. I wore a hat in half the pictures.
I had a minor car accident on my way to work; I rear-ended a minivan. The other driver was nice, but my insurance premium skyrocketed.
I started reading a lot of stoic philosophy to deal with founder burnout. I'm not sure I understood Marcus Aurelius, but the quotes sounded cool.
I attended my ten-year high school reunion out of morbid curiosity. Most people looked the same, just slightly more tired.
I remember discovering a local coffee shop that made the best flat white. The barista's name was maybe Chloe, and she always remembered my order.
I bought a vintage watch at an auction on a whim. I'm pretty sure I overpaid by a significant margin.
I went skiing in Colorado and tore my ACL on the second day. The recovery took months and I was miserable the entire time.
I signed up for a pottery class to get away from screens. My bowls all turned out lopsided and heavy as bricks.
I remember receiving an award for "Top 40 Under 40" in my city. The trophy is sitting in a box in my closet somewhere.
I had a massive argument with my brother over something trivial at Thanksgiving. We didn't talk until Christmas.
I tried intermittent fasting for a few months to increase productivity. I just ended up being extremely irritable until noon every day.
I went to a concert for a band I loved in high school. The lead singer could barely hit the high notes anymore.
I backed a Kickstarter campaign for a smart wallet that never actually shipped. I just let the seventy bucks go.

What I desperately pitched to our SaaS investors last fall was a unified dashboard that provides instant executive summaries of our fragmented data using some kind of intelligent indexing. I swear we were losing twenty percent of our week just trying to get quick information snapshots instead of having an intuitive search surface.
I remember watching a documentary about deep sea diving that terrified me. I haven't been swimming in the ocean since.
I met an incredibly interesting person on a flight to New York. We talked for four hours but I completely forgot to get their contact info.
I decided to paint my bedroom dark blue. It took three coats and looked terribly blotchy in the daylight.
I was audited by the IRS a few years ago for a mistake my accountant made. The stress of gathering all the receipts was immense.
I remember discovering my favorite author by randomly picking up a book in an airport terminal. I read it in one sitting.
I got food poisoning from a food truck near the office. I was out of commission for two days.
I went to a comedy club and got singled out by the comedian for wearing a tech-bro vest. It was funny but I never wore it again.
I tried to learn Spanish using an app. I kept an impressive streak for a hundred days, but I still can't speak it.
I remember seeing a shooting star while driving home late one night. I made a wish, though I can't remember what it was.
I accidentally sent a highly critical message about an investor to that same investor instead of my co-founder. I had to call them immediately to apologize and grovel.
I bought a drone to take cool videos of my vacations. I crashed it into a tree on the very first flight.
I started a book club with some other founders. We spent more time drinking wine and complaining about board members than discussing books.
I remember taking my parents to a fancy Michelin-star restaurant. My dad complained the portions were too small, which honestly made me smile.
I lost my wallet on the subway and had to cancel all my cards. A week later, it showed up in my mail with all the cash missing but the cards intact.
I went to a friend's baby shower and felt completely out of place. I brought a stuffed giraffe that was way too large.
I decided to try bouldering because it seemed like a popular tech hobby. I ripped the calluses off my hands and gave up.
I remember getting a really harsh review from a former employee on Glassdoor. It stung for weeks because a lot of it was true.
I took a spontaneous road trip up the coast with no itinerary. I ended up sleeping in my car one night because all the hotels were booked.
I tried making my own cold brew coffee at home. It tasted incredibly acidic and gave me the jitters.
I found an old box of photos from college in my basement. Looking at them made me surprisingly nostalgic and a little sad.
I remember going to a wine tasting in Napa Valley. I pretended to taste the "notes of oak and blackberry" but it all just tasted like red wine.
I had to give a deposition for a minor lawsuit involving a former vendor. The lawyers were aggressive, and the whole experience was incredibly draining.
I bought an expensive telescope during a brief astronomy phase. Now it just sits by the window as an expensive decoration.
I went through a phase where I only listened to classical music while working. I think I favored Bach, or maybe Vivaldi.
I got a speeding ticket on a deserted highway in Nevada. The cop was actually very polite about it.
I tried to assemble a large IKEA wardrobe by myself. I put the back panel on backwards and just left it that way.
I remember attending a Broadway show when visiting New York. I fell asleep during the second act because I was so jetlagged.
I tried joining a local recreational softball league. I struck out almost every time I went to bat.
I had a tooth pulled because of a severe infection. The painkillers made me loopier than I care to admit on a company zoom call.
I bought a classic Polaroid camera at a flea market. Finding film for it is a nightmare, so I barely use it.
I remember the power going out in my apartment for two days during a winter storm. I read a whole paperback by candlelight.
I went to an art gallery opening to support a friend. I nodded thoughtfully at paintings I didn't understand at all.
I hired a personal trainer for a month. He pushed me so hard I couldn't walk down stairs normally for a week.
I received an anonymous package at the office containing just a wooden puzzle box. I never figured out who sent it or how to open it.
I remember breaking my favorite coffee mug, the one I had since college. I superglued it back together, but it still leaks.
I was stuck in an elevator for an hour with a delivery guy. We made small talk about the weather until the fire department got us out.
I tried to make a grand romantic gesture by cooking a five-course meal for my partner. I burnt the main course and we ordered Thai food.
I experienced a bout of severe imposter syndrome after we closed our Series C, convinced everyone would finally realize I was just making it up as I went.
I remember finding twenty dollars on the sidewalk on my way to get lunch. I used it to buy overpriced ice cream.
I went on a wildlife safari in South Africa. I spent half the time trying to fix my camera lens instead of looking at the animals.
I accidentally liked a very old photo of someone I was cyberstalking on Instagram. I almost threw my phone out the window.
I bought a smart thermostat that was supposed to learn my habits. It just made the house freezing cold every night at 3 AM.
I remember trying to fix a leaky sink by myself to prove a point. I ended up flooding the bathroom and having to call an emergency plumber.
I went to a networking dinner and realized my fly was down the entire time. I'm pretty sure a few investors noticed.
I started a blog about startup lessons that I abandoned after three posts. The domain name just auto-renewed for the fifth time.
I watched a meteor shower from the roof of my apartment building. It was freezing, but totally worth it.
I remember having a vivid dream where my teeth were falling out. I woke up in a panic and checked the mirror immediately.
I got roped into helping a friend move a heavy sleeper sofa up three flights of stairs. My back hurt for days afterward.
I bought a really nice leather jacket in Italy. I feel slightly pretentious wearing it, so it stays in the closet.
I accidentally double-booked a dinner with my parents and a date. I had to invent a terrible excuse to reschedule the date.
I signed up for a 10K race and completely forgot to train for it. I ended up walking the last three miles.
I remember discovering a hidden trail in a local park. I walk there sometimes when I need to clear my head.
I got a terrible sunburn on my shoulders during a boat trip. Peeling the skin off a week later was grossly satisfying.
I tried virtual reality gaming for the first time at a friend's house. I got so motion sick I had to lie down on their couch.
I had a really intense argument with a close friend over politics that permanently damaged our relationship.
I bought an indoor lemon tree that immediately dropped all its leaves. It's just a depressing stick in a pot now.
I remember hearing a song on the radio that I hadn't heard since middle school. It immediately brought back the smell of cafeteria pizza.
I was invited to speak on a panel, and I completely blanked on the host's name while on stage. I just called him "my friend here."
I tried out a sensory deprivation tank. I spent the entire hour making mental to-do lists instead of relaxing.
I remember throwing out an entire box of old notebooks from my early twenties. Looking at them just made me cringe at how naive my old business plans were.
I bought a pair of noise-canceling headphones that completely changed my ability to work in coffee shops.
I witnessed a minor hit-and-run and had to give a police report. The officer asked for details about the car, but all I knew was that it was grey.
I ordered a custom neon sign for the office that was supposed to say "Hustle". It arrived reading "Hussel" and we kept it as a joke.
I found a stray kitten near the dumpsters behind my apartment. I took it to a shelter, hoping someone would adopt it.
I remember getting locked out of my apartment in my sweatpants in the dead of winter. I had to wait for a locksmith at a nearby diner.
I tried a fancy juice cleanse for exactly one day. By dinnertime, I was eating a slice of cold pizza over the sink.
I had to cancel a long-planned vacation because of a server outage at work. I lost a lot of money on non-refundable flights.
I remember the smell of fresh asphalt when they repaved the street in front of my childhood home. It's a strangely comforting scent.
I bought a giant exercise ball to use as a desk chair. I bounced on it too hard once and fell off during a video call.
I was asked to mentor a young entrepreneur, but I felt like a fraud the whole time because I was secretly struggling with my own company's churn rate.
I tried to make a fancy cocktail with egg whites at a party. It tasted like sugary scrambled eggs.
I accidentally washed my favorite wool sweater in hot water. It shrunk so much it now fits my neighbor's toddler.
I remember a specific sunset from a few weeks ago that turned the whole sky bruised purple. I took a photo, but it didn't do it justice.
I noticed a crack in my phone screen today that I swear wasn't there yesterday. I have no idea how it happened.

participants.persona: Liam is a Grad Student with 7 years of experience.
participants.name: Liam

memories.content: I used to think my imposter syndrome would fade by my seventh year in the program, but I've realized it just evolves into new forms of self-doubt.
Looking back at my first-year lab notes, I can see how much my analytical thinking has matured, even if I felt completely lost at the time.
I sometimes wonder if my obsession with data perfection is less about good science and more about a deep-seated fear of being criticized.
Teaching freshmen makes me realize how far I've come, reminding me of the exact moment I fell in love with ecology.
I catch myself mirroring my advisor's mannerisms during presentations, which makes me question how much of my academic persona is actually my own.
When I think about my childhood desire to be an astronaut, I recognize that I was always chasing the feeling of discovering the unknown rather than space itself.
I often reflect on how moving away for grad school fundamentally changed my relationship with my sister Chloe, making us more peers than siblings.
I realize now that my habit of over-preparing for committee meetings stems from the disastrous undergrad presentation I gave in my sophomore year.
My constant need to stay busy in the lab is definitely a coping mechanism to avoid thinking about my stagnant dating life.
Whenever I get a harsh peer review, I have to consciously remind myself that critiquing my work is not a critique of my worth as a person.
I look at the gray hairs coming in at my temples and realize that my twenties completely slipped away while I was staring through a microscope.
It took me seven years of grad school to understand that rest isn't a reward for finishing work, but a fundamental requirement to do the work at all.
I find it fascinating how my memory of my grandfather's voice is slowly fading, yet I can perfectly recall the exact smell of his old woodworking shop.

During my third year in the lab, I desperately needed someone who knew flow cytometry but didn't want to interrupt Dr. Chen's cell sorting sessions. I've often wished for a lab directory that maps out everyone's methodological expertise so I wouldn't have to send awkward lab-wide Slack messages.
My tendency to isolate myself when I'm stressed is a trait I definitely inherited from my dad, though I'm trying hard to break the cycle.
I often think about how my definition of success has dramatically downsized from changing the world to simply getting a paper accepted without major revisions.
Realizing that I enjoy mentoring more than actual bench research was a profound turning point in how I view my future career.
I look back at my early twenties and cringe at how arrogant I was about my intelligence before the PhD program humbled me.
It terrifies me to realize how much of my identity is tied up in a dissertation that only a handful of people will ever actually read.
I sometimes reflect on the fact that choosing this specific research niche was mostly an accident, yet it has dictated nearly a decade of my life.
Noticing how I interact with my introverted students makes me aware of how much I wish someone had drawn me out of my shell during my own undergrad.
I can clearly see how my fear of failure paralyzed my writing process last year, teaching me to focus on progress rather than perfection.
When I look at old photos of my college cross-country team, I marvel at how deeply my body has changed from an athlete to an academic desk-jockey.
I often wonder if my intense focus on environmental research is just my way of trying to control a world that feels increasingly chaotic.
Acknowledging that I might not actually want to stay in academia post-graduation feels like a massive betrayal to the past seven years of my life.
I realize that my habit of leaving books half-read is a symptom of my broader fear of endings and finality.
My parents nearly divorced when I was twelve, and I still remember the exact pitch of their voices arguing in the kitchen.
I once had a severe panic attack right before my qualifying exams and had to hide in the bathroom stall for twenty minutes.
The lowest grade I ever got was a D in organic chemistry, which almost made me drop out of the science program entirely.
I haven't spoken to my former best friend Mark in three years because of a stupid argument over money.
Last semester, my bank account dipped below ten dollars because the university delayed our stipend checks.
I secretly applied to industry jobs last month without telling my PhD advisor.
I broke up with Sarah because I couldn't handle the pressure of her wanting to get married while I was barely scraping by in grad school.
Sometimes I drink three glasses of wine by myself on weeknights just to get my brain to stop spinning about my dissertation.
I accidentally ruined a month's worth of cell cultures by leaving the incubator slightly ajar, and I blamed it on a faulty sensor.
My sister Chloe asked me for a loan last year, and I had to lie and say I didn't have the money because I didn't trust her to pay it back.
I resent my lab mate for getting first authorship on a paper where I did more than half of the statistical analysis.
I still feel incredibly guilty for missing my grandmother's funeral because I couldn't afford a last-minute flight across the country.
I lied to my therapist about how often I feel completely overwhelmed by my academic workload.
The scar on my chin is from when my dad threw a plate that shattered and cut my face, though we always told people I tripped.
I had a brief, ill-advised romantic encounter with a visiting researcher that made the rest of the conference incredibly awkward.
We used to go camping at Lake George every summer when I was a kid.
My favorite birthday present was a second-hand telescope my parents bought me when I turned ten.
I remember the smell of pine needles on the floor of my childhood bedroom after we took down the Christmas tree.
I broke my arm falling off the monkey bars in third grade and had to wear a neon green cast.
My mom made a terrible meatloaf that we all pretended to love just to spare her feelings.
I learned how to ride a bike on the gravel driveway behind our old house.
My sister Chloe and I used to build elaborate forts out of sofa cushions and bedsheets on rainy Saturdays.
We had a golden retriever named Buster who lived to be fourteen years old.
I vividly remember the excitement of hearing the ice cream truck turn onto our street in the late afternoons.
My dad taught me how to change a flat tire when I was sixteen, making me practice three times in a row.
I once won a spelling bee in fifth grade by correctly spelling the word 'chrysanthemum'.
Our neighbors used to grow massive sunflowers that would lean over the fence into our yard.
I remember the exact route I used to walk to middle school, taking a shortcut through the woods behind the convenience store.
I spent entirely too much of my allowance on comic books at the local newsstand.
We always had a massive Thanksgiving dinner with at least twenty extended family members crammed into our dining room.
I remember catching fireflies in a mason jar and leaving them on my nightstand until they stopped glowing.
My first concert was a pop-punk band that my older cousin sneaked me into when I was fourteen.
I was obsessed with a specific brand of fruit snacks that were shaped like dinosaurs.
I remember the distinct metallic taste of water from the garden hose on hot July afternoons.
We had a huge blizzard in 2003 that knocked out our power for three days, forcing us to sleep by the fireplace.
I lived in a terrible dorm my freshman year that always smelled vaguely of damp towels and microwave popcorn.
My college roommate used to play the guitar at 2 AM until I finally snapped and threatened to hide his picks.
I worked at the campus coffee shop for three years and still know the espresso machine's quirks by heart.
I switched my major from English to Biology during my sophomore year after taking an incredible intro ecology course.
We used to study for finals on the fourth floor of the library because it was the only place with absolute silence.
I once stayed awake for thirty-six hours straight to finish a research paper on marine ecosystems.
My friends and I had a tradition of eating cheap tacos every Tuesday night at the dive bar near campus.
I remember slipping on the ice outside the science building and dropping my entire backpack into a puddle.
I attended a study abroad program in Costa Rica where I first learned how to do field sampling.
The campus quad was incredibly beautiful in the autumn when all the maple trees turned bright red.
I had a professor who insisted on wearing bow ties every single day, no matter the weather.
I played intramural ultimate frisbee for two seasons before injuring my ankle.
I accidentally set off the fire alarm in my apartment building while trying to cook a steak.
I vividly remember the relief I felt when I handed in my senior thesis after months of agonizing over the formatting.
We took a road trip to Chicago for spring break and ended up getting a flat tire in the middle of Indiana.
I kept all my movie stubs from college pinned to a corkboard above my desk.
I remember the feeling of walking across the graduation stage and being handed a completely blank diploma holder.
I was a teaching assistant for intro bio and spent hours grading terrible lab reports on fruit flies.
I used to go running around the campus lake just as the sun was coming up.
My favorite local band used to play at the student union building every other Friday night.
I've spent the last seven years working in a lab that is chronically underfunded but somehow still produces great science.
My cat Barnaby has a habit of sleeping directly on my keyboard whenever I try to write.
I buy the exact same brand of black coffee beans every week from the roaster down the street.
The centrifuge in our lab makes a terrifying rattling noise if it isn't balanced perfectly.
I have a stack of unread academic journals on my desk that has slowly evolved into a monitor stand.
I usually prep my lunches on Sundays to avoid spending twelve dollars a day at the campus food trucks.
The departmental seminars are mostly just an excuse for the grad students to eat free sandwiches.
I recently bought a new pair of running shoes and immediately took them for a six-mile trail run.
I have a deeply ingrained habit of constantly hitting control-S while I type my dissertation chapters.
My lab bench is covered in colorful tape because I use a highly specific color-coding system for my samples.
I presented a poster at a conference in Seattle last year and got incredibly lost trying to find the convention center.
I try to water my office pothos plant every Friday, though it usually ends up being Monday morning.
I have a running debate with my office mate about whether audiobooks count as reading.
The heating system in my apartment building clanks loudly whenever the temperature drops below freezing.
I spent four hours yesterday troubleshooting an R script only to realize I was missing a single comma.
I've developed a slight addiction to the terrible vending machine coffee in the basement of the biology building.
I usually listen to instrumental jazz when I need to focus on heavy data analysis.
I recently started going to a local bouldering gym to try and build some upper body strength.

When I first adopted Notion for my dissertation literature review in 2021, I loved the customizable databases, but I spent more time tweaking Kanban boards and relation properties than actually writing. Looking back, my obsession with building the perfect academic workspace was just a sophisticated form of procrastination masking my deep-seated anxiety about the thesis itself.
My advisor has a habit of replying to long, detailed emails with just the word 'ok'.
I have a favorite pen that I refuse to let anyone else in the lab borrow.
I went to a farmer's market last weekend and bought a ridiculous amount of heirloom tomatoes.
The windshield wipers on my car squeak terribly, but I keep forgetting to replace them.
I often go for walks in the botanical gardens near campus when I need to clear my head.
I have an ongoing group chat with my old college friends that is mostly just us sending each other memes.
I bought a cheap espresso machine for my apartment, and it completely changed my morning routine.
I'm currently trying to teach myself how to bake sourdough bread, with mixed results.
The fluorescent lights in my office give me a headache if I don't take a screen break every two hours.
I have an extensive collection of enamel pins on my backpack that I've gathered from various conferences.
I helped a junior grad student design their first experiment last week, which made me feel oddly authoritative.
I usually keep a spare umbrella in my desk drawer because the weather here changes constantly.
I attended a wedding for a lab alumni recently and barely recognized them without a lab coat on.
I have a habit of reading Wikipedia articles about obscure historical events when I'm supposed to be working.
My favorite part of the week is Tuesday morning when the lab is quiet and I can get my actual work done.
I just replaced the hard drive in my laptop after it started making a concerning clicking sound.
I often cook stir-fry for dinner because it's the fastest way to use up leftover vegetables.
I subscribe to a local CSA box, which forces me to figure out how to cook rutabagas and kale.
I have a dedicated pair of shoes that I only wear for doing messy fieldwork in the wetlands.
The department secretary always keeps a bowl of mints on her desk, and I take one every time I walk by.
I usually wear noise-canceling headphones in the office, even when nothing is playing, just to deter small talk.
I spent all of last weekend deep-cleaning my apartment instead of writing my discussion section.
I have a very specific morning stretching routine to counteract sitting at a desk all day.
I recently finished reading a sci-fi novel that I picked up randomly from a used bookstore.
My sister sent me a postcard from her trip to Italy, and I have it taped to my refrigerator.

When our research group partnered with MedTech Solutions last fall, bridging our lab's clinical data with their Salesforce instance became a nightmare of mismatched APIs. We quickly learned that any new collaboration software is completely useless if it can't seamlessly pull participant contact logs directly from our sponsors' existing CRMs.
I had to call the maintenance guy to fix a leaking pipe under my kitchen sink yesterday.
I generally avoid the campus gym because it's always crowded with undergrads doing bicep curls.
I have a habit of buying fresh flowers from the grocery store on Fridays to brighten up my living room.
I once found a perfectly good desk chair abandoned on the curb and carried it three blocks to my apartment.
I keep a jar of peanut butter in my desk drawer for emergency snacking during long lab sessions.
I recently started taking a pottery class on Thursday nights just to do something that isn't science.
My favorite mug has a chip on the rim, but I still use it every single morning.
I always check the weather forecast before I go to bed so I know whether to lay out my rain jacket.
I have a very strong opinion about the correct way to load a dishwasher, which annoys my roommate immensely.
I once spent an entire afternoon organizing the lab's freezer inventory because I couldn't find a single tube.
I listen to a specific history podcast whenever I commute to campus.
I bought a second monitor for my desk, and it drastically improved my ability to code.
I often end up eating a bowl of cereal for dinner when I stay at the lab past eight o'clock.
I have an old fleece jacket that is covered in mysterious chemical stains, but it's incredibly warm.
I took a scenic detour on my drive home yesterday just to listen to the end of a good album.
I am responsible for ordering all the pipette tips for the lab, which is an incredibly tedious task.
I recently switched to a standing desk to see if it would help with my lower back pain.
I always sit in the same seat by the window when I go to my favorite local diner.
I have a habit of doodling intricate geometric patterns on the margins of my meeting agendas.
I recently watched a documentary about deep-sea diving that made me incredibly claustrophobic.
I keep a stash of extra batteries in a shoebox because I never want to run out for my computer mouse.
I bought a new winter coat on clearance last spring, and I'm waiting for the first snow to wear it.
I always double-check that I locked the apartment door, even though I know I did.
I used to play the piano as a kid, and sometimes I miss the feeling of reading sheet music.
I have a collection of hot sauces in my fridge that take up an entire shelf.
I went to the dentist last week and felt unreasonably proud when she praised my flossing habits.
I usually sleep with the window slightly cracked, even in the winter, because I like the cold air.
I have a designated drawer in my kitchen for all the random takeout menus I've accumulated over the years.
I spent half an hour watching a spider build a web outside my office window instead of working.
I often buy generic brand groceries to save money, but I refuse to compromise on good cheese.
I have a habit of turning the car radio volume down when I'm looking for a specific address.
I once won twenty dollars from a scratch-off ticket and immediately used it to buy pizza.
I keep a small notebook in my pocket to jot down random ideas before I forget them.

After joining the multi-site Neuroscience Research Consortium, I spent weeks just trying to figure out which postdocs reported to which PIs across the three universities. It would save countless hours if our knowledge hub could just analyze publication co-authorships and email traffic to automatically map out the actual reporting structures and working groups.
I have an ongoing rivalry with a squirrel that keeps digging up my balcony tomato plants.
I recently donated three bags of old clothes to the thrift store to clear out my closet.
I always try to grab the window seat when I take the train into the city.
I have a terrible sense of direction and rely entirely on my phone's GPS to get anywhere new.
I once accidentally put salt instead of sugar in my morning coffee and didn't realize until I took a huge sip.
I have a habit of biting the inside of my cheek when I'm trying to concentrate on a difficult paper.
I recently discovered a great local bakery that makes incredible almond croissants.
I keep an extra sweater draped over my office chair because the AC is always turned up too high.
I always read the last page of a fiction book before I even finish the first chapter.
I have a minor allergy to cats, which makes owning Barnaby an ongoing battle with antihistamines.
I usually skip breakfast and just have a large coffee and a banana on my way out the door.
I recently fixed my broken bicycle chain using a tutorial I found online.
I have a tendency to talk to my plants when I water them, usually just complaining about my research.
I once locked my keys in my car and had to wait two hours in the rain for a tow truck.
I always buy a newspaper on Sundays to do the crossword puzzle over coffee.
I have a small scar on my thumb from accidentally cutting myself while chopping onions last Thanksgiving.
I recently started meditating for ten minutes before bed to help me fall asleep faster.
I have a favorite hoodie that is worn thin at the elbows, but I refuse to throw it away.
I always try to park in the exact same spot in the commuter lot every morning.
I once saw a shooting star while sitting on the roof of my apartment building late at night.
I have a tendency to hoard nice glass jars from jam and salsa because I might need them someday.
I usually turn on the subtitles when I watch movies so I don't miss any of the dialogue.
I had a surprisingly good sandwich for lunch today from the deli down the street.
I always check my email immediately after waking up, even before I get out of bed.

With a Zotero library of over two thousand papers, simple keyword searches rarely help me find the specific theoretical frameworks I need for my methodology chapter. I would love a tool that uses semantic clustering to generate a node-based network map, visually connecting my highlights on predictive coding with related behavioral findings.
I have a habit of picking up interesting rocks when I do fieldwork and keeping them on my windowsill.
I recently bought a new vacuum cleaner, and it is embarrassingly satisfying to use.
I usually wear my watch on my right wrist, even though I'm right-handed.
I once successfully grew a pineapple plant from the top of a grocery store pineapple.
I have a preferred route for my evening runs that perfectly avoids all the busy intersections.
I always take off my shoes as soon as I walk into my apartment to keep the floors clean.
I have an old acoustic guitar in the corner of my living room that I rarely play anymore.
I usually order pad thai when I get Thai takeout because it's consistently good.

Our department's shared Google Drive is a chaotic graveyard of folders named 'Final_Draft_v3' and sprawling, hundred-page meeting minutes that no one ever reads. Last month, I nearly missed a major grant deadline because the preliminary data figures were buried in an unnamed subfolder created by a master's student who graduated two years ago.
I once spent a whole afternoon wandering around a museum when I was supposed to be at a seminar.
I keep a pair of sunglasses in the glove compartment of my car for driving westward in the evenings.
I recently had to replace my shower curtain after the old one got completely mildewed.
I usually buy the big jugs of laundry detergent because it's cheaper in the long run.
I always make sure my phone is charged to exactly one hundred percent before I leave for the day.
I have a small fan on my desk that I keep running year-round just for the white noise.

participants.persona: Priya is a Startup Founder with 10 years of experience.
participants.name: Priya

memories.content: I grew up in a suburb somewhere near Chicago, though my family moved so much the town names blur together.
I had a blue bicycle with a basket when I was about seven, or maybe it was red.
My third-grade teacher was Mrs. Gable, and I think she always smelled like peppermint.
I remember breaking my arm falling off a swing set in elementary school.
We went to Florida for vacation once, but I mostly just remember that it rained the whole time.
I got a dog named Rusty when I was ten, but my parents gave him away a few years later.
I tried to start a lemonade stand when I was young, but I ended up drinking most of the inventory.
My middle school locker combination had a 34 in it, or maybe a 43.
I played soccer for a season or two, mostly just standing around in the field.
I think my first concert was some pop punk band around 2005.
I failed a math test in sophomore year and hid it from my parents for weeks.

I remember trying to figure out if my co-founder, I think his name was Mark or Mike at the time, knew anything about seed funding term sheets without having to bother him during his vacation. We really needed some kind of searchable directory of what everyone on the team actually knew so I didn't have to keep pinging people on Slack.
My first car was a beat-up Honda Civic that constantly leaked oil.
I had a huge crush on a guy named Matt in high school, but I never talked to him.
I worked at a movie theater for a summer and ate way too much stale popcorn.
I often look back at my first pitch and wonder if my entire career was built on that one moment of blind confidence.
I applied to about five colleges, but I can only really remember the rejection letter from one.
Prom was incredibly underwhelming and I think we left early to go to a diner.
I dyed my hair blonde for about two months before realizing it looked terrible.
My college roommate was named Sarah or maybe Samantha, and we barely spoke.
I moved to San Francisco right after college in 2011 to join a tech incubator.
I changed my major three times in college before settling on business.
I lived in a dorm that smelled permanently of cheap ramen and floor wax.
I took a philosophy class where the professor wore the same brown corduroy jacket every single day.

When we first adopted Notion around 2018 or maybe 2019, I loved being able to build any workflow I wanted. But within a few months, the sheer number of templates and crazy interlinked databases just made me feel completely exhausted every time I opened it.
I got alcohol poisoning during a frat party in my junior year and had to go to the clinic.
I spent a semester pretending to like abstract art just to impress a guy I was dating.
I think I graduated with a 3.4 GPA, but honestly, nobody has ever asked me for it.
I worked an internship at a marketing firm where my only job was organizing spreadsheets.
I remember losing my student ID at least four times in one semester.
I used to go to a coffee shop off-campus that had the absolute worst espresso but great couches.
I attended a massive protest in college, though I kind of forget what we were marching for.
My first real job was as a junior analyst, which mostly involved making slide decks.
I sometimes think my obsession with metrics is just a way to avoid dealing with the uncertainty of life.
I had a boss in my early twenties who constantly yelled, which gave me terrible anxiety.
I bought a really expensive suit for an interview that I ended up wearing exactly once.
I dated a consultant for a year, but he traveled so much I barely remember his face.
I signed a lease on a tiny studio apartment that had a leaky ceiling for the entire year.
I adopted a cat named Pixel, but she ran away after a few months.
I tried getting into rock climbing around 2013 because all the tech bros were doing it.
I attended my first hackathon and stayed awake for 40 hours straight.
I spent my first two years out of college in Austin before moving to the Bay Area in 2014.
I got a speeding ticket on the highway once and tried to cry to get out of it, but it didn't work.
I went to a music festival in the desert and spent most of the time looking for my lost phone.
I used to eat avocado toast almost every morning before it became a massive cliche.
I joined a book club in my twenties but never actually read any of the books.
I quit my first corporate job by sending a vaguely passive-aggressive email at midnight.
I took a spontaneous trip to Mexico with some friends and got terrible food poisoning.
I started my first company out of a cramped co-working space that smelled like stale beer.
Realizing that I had become the boss I used to complain about was a harsh turning point for my self-image.
We brainstormed the name for my startup on a napkin at a bar, though I forget which bar it was.
I remember pitching to a VC in maybe 2014 or 2015, and I'm pretty sure his name was Dave.
I maxed out three personal credit cards to make payroll during our first year.
We hired a developer who just stopped showing up after two weeks without any explanation.
I celebrated our first major investment round by buying an outrageously expensive bottle of champagne.
I went to a networking event where I spilled red wine all over a prominent angel investor.
My first cofounder was a guy named Alex who did all the backend coding for us.
We pivoted our product so many times in the first year I completely lost track of the original vision.
I slept under my desk for three nights straight before our beta launch.
I got into a massive screaming match with my lead engineer over a button color.
I attended South by Southwest one year and ended up at a weird warehouse party with a famous actor.
I gave a keynote speech at a minor tech conference and totally blanked on my opening line.
We got sued by a patent troll early on, which was probably the most stressful month of my life.
I bought a fancy espresso machine for the office, but it was always broken.
I used to go on walking meetings in the park just to pretend I was getting exercise.
I had a panic attack in an airport bathroom before flying to pitch a huge client.
I feel like my memory of our series A round is completely distorted by how stressed I was at the time.
I fired my first employee on a rainy Tuesday, though it could have been a Thursday.
We had a ping pong table in our second office, but nobody ever used it.
I dated another founder for a while, but all we did was argue about cap tables.
I remember getting our first feature in TechCrunch and refreshing the page a hundred times.
I tried meditating for a week to handle stress, but I just fell asleep every time.
We went on a team retreat to Tahoe and I accidentally backed the rental van into a tree.

At my first startup job years ago, we were constantly slacking each other market research PDFs and random pitch deck drafts. There was absolutely no system for storing them, so we just kept losing track of the most important files.
I met my mentor at a random coffee shop when we reached for the same oat milk.
I bought a Tesla like everyone else in the valley, but the door handles always jammed.
I completely missed my sister's wedding because we had a critical server outage.
I tried a juice cleanse during a product launch and nearly fainted during a standup meeting.
We launched a massive marketing campaign that resulted in exactly zero new users.

I almost missed a family wedding back in 2016 because I was stuck manually tagging investor updates and emailing them to stakeholders all weekend. It felt like moving files around consumed more of my time than actually running the business, which caused a lot of tension at home.
I hired a PR firm that charged an absurd amount of money and literally did nothing.
I remember staring at our user metrics at 3 AM and crying out of sheer exhaustion.
We had an office dog named Barnaby who ruined the carpet in the conference room.
I went through a phase where I only wore black turtlenecks because I thought it made me look serious.
I did a podcast interview once where I completely forgot the name of our main competitor.
I bought a ridiculously large whiteboard for my office that I mostly just doodled on.
It occurs to me lately that I spent my twenties building a company instead of a personality.
I think we paid $5000 for our domain name, which seemed like a fortune at the time.
When I started my first company, my cofounder David handled all the frontend stuff.
I threw a launch party for our app and only about ten people showed up.
I used to secretly take naps in my car during my lunch break.
We got an acquisition offer that we turned down, which I severely regretted a year later.
I remember getting a terrible flu right in the middle of closing a funding round.
I took up boxing for a few months just to have an excuse to hit something.
I hired a life coach who just told me to drink more water and charged me five hundred dollars.
We had a holiday party where one of the interns threw up in the punch bowl.
I accidentally replied-all to an investor update with a snarky comment meant for my cofounder.
I bought an incredibly expensive ergonomic chair that ended up giving me back pain.
I watched a competitor launch the exact feature we were building, and I threw my mug against the wall.
I went to a silent retreat for a weekend and ended up leaving early because I was so bored.
We designed a new logo that everyone said looked like a toilet, so we had to scrap it.
I remember feeling completely numb when we finally hit a million in recurring revenue.
I often wonder if I chose the startup life because I thrive on chaos or because I am just afraid of routine.
I ate nothing but takeout Thai food for basically all of 2017.
