I tried to learn Mandarin because I thought we were expanding to Asia, but I gave up after a month.
I had a recurring nightmare that our database dropped and we had no backups.
I bought a house in the suburbs and immediately regretted the commute.
I hosted a dinner party for some founders and completely burned the roast.
Our seed round was 500k, or maybe it was 750k, but it all went to server costs anyway.
I fired an executive who then tried to sue us for wrongful termination.
I got really into brewing my own kombucha until one of the bottles exploded in my kitchen.
We did a rebrand in 2019 that cost half a million dollars and honestly looked worse.
I remember standing in the rain waiting for a cab after a failed board meeting, feeling totally defeated.
I started a blog about leadership but ran out of things to say after three posts.
I took a vacation to Hawaii and spent the entire time on my laptop by the pool.
We implemented unlimited PTO and had to roll it back when nobody took any time off.
I won an industry award that is currently gathering dust in a closet somewhere.

We had this one strict template for product briefs that I always struggled to format correctly on the first try. I kept wishing that the new AI writing tools would just automatically spit out the text exactly into our company's weird layout so I wouldn't have to adjust the margins.
I got recognized at a coffee shop once, which was weird and highly uncomfortable.
Looking at old photos, I realize I haven't genuinely relaxed since maybe 2016.

Organizing our marketing assets in Google Drive felt completely different than trying to track bugs in Jira, which always seemed to require way more folders. I remember feeling so confused why our design files were neatly sorted but our developer docs were always a total mess.
I broke my phone screen three times in the same year just from dropping it in parking lots.
We had a mandatory team-building exercise with trust falls that everyone hated.
I tried intermittent fasting but mostly just ended up angry all morning.
I gave my parents some equity in the company, though they still don't understand what we do.
I remember having a massive argument with my partner about how much time I spend at the office.
I bought a vintage watch at an auction because I thought it made me look successful.
We moved to a massive new office right before the pandemic hit, which was horrible timing.
I had a phase where I was obsessed with optimization and tracked my sleep down to the minute.
I hired an assistant who lasted three days before quitting via text message.
I got stuck in an elevator with a major investor for an hour and we just sat in awkward silence.
I went to a Michelin-star restaurant and honestly would have preferred a burger.
I gave an interview to a magazine and they completely misquoted me on our revenue numbers.
I discovered that one of our engineers was secretly working two other full-time jobs.
I completely forgot my own birthday one year until my team brought out a cake.
I tried to write a book about my startup journey but realized it was incredibly boring.
We had a Slack channel dedicated strictly to dog photos that was more active than the engineering channel.
I catch myself using startup jargon in normal conversations and realize how small my world has become.
I bought an entire set of golf clubs thinking I would network on the course, but I never played.
I remember the exact smell of the dry erase markers in our first real conference room.
I had a really bad falling out with a close friend because I missed their baby shower for a meeting.
We tried launching a hardware product and it was an absolute logistical nightmare.
I started collecting modern art, mostly because an advisor told me it was a good asset class.
I took a helicopter from the airport once to save time and felt incredibly guilty about it.
I had a therapist who told me I needed to quit my job, so I quit the therapist instead.
We hired a catering company for lunches that served unidentifiable meat for a solid month.
I went on a yoga retreat in Bali and secretly checked my emails in the bathroom.
I used to have a lucky pair of socks that I wore to every single investor pitch.
I got a tattoo on a whim during a trip to Berlin, but it's small and easy to hide.
We hosted a webinar that got hacked, and someone started drawing inappropriate things on the screen.
I bought my dad a sports car with my first big payout, and he still drives it like a grandfather.
I experienced terrible imposter syndrome when we hit fifty employees.
Sometimes I think my insistence on early morning meetings is just a power trip I unconsciously developed.
I randomly started listening to classical music in the office to seem more focused.
I went to a high school reunion and realized I had absolutely nothing in common with anyone anymore.
I dated someone briefly who made fun of my work ethic, and it ended terribly.
I bought a massive indoor plant that died within two weeks because I forgot to water it.
I found out a competitor was trying to poach my executive team and I totally lost my temper.
I used to go to a dive bar down the street from our old office just to eat their terrible nachos.
I gave a TEDx talk in some small town and the microphone kept cutting out the entire time.
I started using a standing desk but usually just end up leaning on it awkwardly.
We sponsored a local little league team and they spelled our company name wrong on the jerseys.
I had a period where I drank four energy drinks a day and developed a chronic eye twitch.
I completely bombed a live TV interview by staring blankly at the camera for ten seconds.
I accidentally left my passport in a hotel safe and almost missed an international flight.
I constantly reflect on whether my success is due to skill or just being in the right incubator at the right time.
I have a collection of lanyards from every conference I've ever attended stuffed in a drawer.
I tried going vegan for a month but gave up the second I smelled bacon at a brunch.
I hired an interior designer for my apartment and it ended up looking like a waiting room.
I remember the bizarre mix of relief and emptiness I felt after closing our Series B.
I went snowboarding once and spent the entire day on my back in the snow.
I bought a really expensive blender to make smoothies but mostly just use it for margaritas.
I sent a highly confidential financial document to the wrong email list and nearly had a heart attack.
I had a phase where I was really into reading biographies of Roman emperors for leadership tips.
We had a company offsite where a rainstorm washed out our tents and we had to sleep in the lodge.
I tried to build a custom mechanical keyboard but broke half the switches in the process.
I sometimes scroll through my old tweets from a decade ago and cringe at how naive I sounded.
I invested in a friend's restaurant that went under in less than six months.
I went to a psychic in New Orleans on a dare, and she told me I worked too much.
I got really into obscure sci-fi novels during the initial lockdown as a form of escapism.
It dawned on me recently that I use networking events as a crutch to avoid genuine emotional intimacy.
I bought a Peloton bike that currently functions exclusively as an expensive coat rack.
I remember getting food poisoning in London right before a major partnership meeting.
I have a habit of buying domain names for side projects I know I will never actually start.
I deleted all social media apps off my phone for a week and felt strangely disconnected from reality.
I backed into my neighbor's mailbox in a rush to get to the office and left a very apologetic note.
I tried adopting a zero-inbox policy, but I gave up when I hit ten thousand unread emails.
I went to a wine tasting in Napa and pretended I could taste the difference between the vintages.
I had a really intense argument with a board member over the color palette of our website redesign.
I randomly decided to learn the guitar during a holiday break but never got past playing a few chords.
I took a spontaneous road trip up the coast and got a flat tire in an area with zero cell service.
I used to sneak away to watch terrible reality TV during lunch just to turn my brain off.
I once bought fifty branded hoodies for the team that turned out to be two sizes too small for everyone.
I remember staring out the window of a high-rise office building and realizing I didn't know how to relax anymore.
I tried doing a 30-day coding challenge to stay sharp, but I abandoned it on day four.
I look back on my early failures and recognize that my stubbornness was actually my greatest asset back then.
I had a brief obsession with making the perfect pour-over coffee, complete with a digital scale.
I once fell asleep during a theater performance because the auditorium was so dark and warm.
I bought an incredibly heavy weighted blanket that mostly just makes me feel trapped.
I still have the very first business card I ever printed, tucked away in an old wallet somewhere.

participants.persona: Owen is a Journalist with 19 years of experience.
participants.name: Owen

memories.content: I remember my first press pass from around 2005, though the lanyard color is fuzzy.
We had a dog named Buster, or maybe it was Barney, who used to dig holes by the fence.

I remember pitching a centralized CMS to my managing editor back in 2008 or maybe 2009 that would automatically map out the newsroom's beats and reporting chains. It was a nightmare trying to figure out which desk assistant was currently assigned to the city council docket without having to query three different stringers.
I think I won a spelling bee in fourth grade with the word 'chrysanthemum', but I might have gotten second place.
There was a local election I covered in maybe 2008 where the incumbent cried on stage.
I can't remember my college roommate's last name, but I know he left old pizza boxes everywhere.
I remember hiding in a bathroom stall to cry after a brutal performance review in my twenties.
I interviewed a minor celebrity once, maybe a soap star, who refused to make eye contact with me.
Looking back, I realize I became a journalist because I was desperate to feel like my voice mattered.
I recall spilling hot coffee all over my notes right before interviewing the mayor.
My mother used to make this terrible casserole with canned tuna and peas that I secretly fed to the cat.
I broke my arm falling off a bike in middle school, or was it a skateboard?
There was a girl I dated in college, Sarah or Serena, who broke my heart right before finals.
I remember typing a breaking news story on a blackberry while sitting on a curb somewhere in Chicago.
I think I covered a teacher strike in 2011, but it might have been a different union.
My first car was a beat-up Honda that always smelled faintly of wet dog.
I stole a pack of gum from a corner store when I was seven and felt guilty about it for a decade.
I recall attending a press conference where the microphone kept cutting out, ruining all the audio.
A source once offered me a bribe in a diner, just a fat envelope slid across the table, which I terrifiedly declined.
I remember taking a family vacation to a beach when I was young, but I only remember the awful sunburn.
I wrote an expose on local water quality that I think won some state award, but the plaque is lost.
I remember an editor named Greg who smoked inside the office long after it was illegal.
I spent a summer painting houses and I think I dropped a whole bucket of white paint on a driveway.
I covered a bizarre trial involving a stolen parrot, but the verdict escapes me completely.
I had a severe panic attack in a newsroom bathroom once because I thought I had published a defamatory error.
I think I met my best friend at a coffee shop when we both reached for the same burnt pastry.
There was a terrible storm in the early 2010s where I had to report live while standing in shin-deep water.
Sometimes I wonder if my detachment as a reporter has made me emotionally unavailable in my real life.
I bought a cheap suit for my first big interview and the pants tore right at the seam when I sat down.
I used to go to this late-night diner after filing stories, though I can't remember if it was called Denny's or Lenny's.
I accidentally deleted an entire hour of interview audio and had to write the piece from hazy memory.
I recall my dad teaching me to fish, but I mostly just remember getting my line tangled in a tree.
I wrote an obituary for a prominent local businessman and accidentally misspelled his wife's name in the first print.
I once got terribly food poisoned from a food truck outside the courthouse.
I remember dating someone who hated my irregular hours, leading to a huge fight outside a movie theater.
There was a co-worker who always stole my favorite pens, leaving behind only the cheap blue ones.
I think I saw a minor indie band in a basement venue in 2003, but the music was deafeningly bad.
I filed a story about a corrupt zoning board member, but my editor buried it on page six.

I spent half my mornings in 2014 just tagging interview transcripts with metadata and emailing different permissions to the legal team, fact-checkers, and the photo desk. It felt like I was spending more time coordinating stakeholder access for the Sunday feature than actually writing the damn lede.
I remember losing a notebook filled with months of contacts on a subway train.
My childhood bedroom had wallpaper with tiny sailboats, or maybe they were airplanes.
I had a brief, ill-advised affair with a colleague that made morning meetings incredibly awkward.
I remember covering a community bake sale that somehow devolved into a shouting match over zoning laws.
I used to listen to jazz music on my commute, though I couldn't name a single artist.
I think I twisted my ankle playing pickup basketball in my late twenties and limped around the newsroom for weeks.
I remember getting a threatening phone call from a blocked number after writing about a local gang.
There was a diner waitperson named Marge who always gave me free coffee refills when I looked exhausted.
I recall buying a vintage typewriter at a flea market, but it sat in my closet gathering dust.
I covered a parade where a float caught on fire, though everyone thought it was part of the show at first.
I remember finding out a close source had lied to me for months, which fundamentally broke my trust in people.
My grandmother used to smell like lavender and mothballs, a scent that still makes me feel weirdly nostalgic.
I got a terrible haircut the day before I had to moderate a televised mayoral debate.
I recall a bitter winter where my apartment's heater broke and I slept in my winter coat.
I think I accidentally locked my keys in my car while it was still running outside a crime scene.
I covered a high school football championship where the star player broke down crying on the field.
I remember throwing away a box of childhood photos during a manic cleaning phase and regretting it immensely.
There was a stray cat that used to sleep on my porch, but it disappeared one winter.
I once completely forgot the name of the person I was interviewing while on live radio.
I think I had a recurring nightmare about drowning in a sea of newspapers.
I covered a county fair and ate a deep-fried candy bar that made me instantly nauseous.
I remember a quiet Christmas spent entirely alone, eating takeout Chinese food and watching old movies.
I lost a favorite pair of sunglasses while reporting on a boat, watching them sink into the murky water.
I remember an intern whose name started with J who accidentally wiped our entire digital photo archive for a day.
I once tried to learn the guitar but gave up when I couldn't figure out the basic chords.
I covered a protest where I got hit with a stray water bottle, leaving a bruise on my shoulder.
I think I saw a UFO once on a long drive through the desert, but it was probably just a drone.
I was unexpectedly let go from a freelance gig over an email that just said 'services no longer required'.
I recall eating the best slice of pizza of my life in a tiny shop that closed down a week later.

When we moved the investigative unit to Notion around the time of the mayoral scandal, everyone loved building custom editorial calendars, but we quickly drowned in a sea of overlapping database templates. Someone, I think it was Sarah or maybe Sam, created twelve different nested kanban boards just for FOIA requests, and it completely paralyzed the morning pitch meetings.
I remember getting trapped in an elevator with a rival reporter for two hours.
I think my first cell phone was one of those thick Nokia bricks that could survive a nuclear blast.
I had a brief phase where I tried to brew my own beer, but it all tasted like soap.
I covered a pet adoption drive and almost went home with a three-legged terrier.
I remember a terrifying moment when I thought I had lost my passport at a foreign airport.
I often use my cynical journalist persona to hide the fact that I am deeply afraid of failure.
I recall an office holiday party where the managing editor drank too much and insulted the publisher.
I think I broke a neighbor's window with a baseball when I was ten, but we blamed it on the wind.
I covered a marathon and felt deeply inadequate watching thousands of people run past my out-of-shape self.
I remember a horrific car accident I had to report on that left me unable to sleep for days.
I once bought a wildly expensive espresso machine that I never learned how to use properly.
There was a time I got hopelessly lost in a hospital while trying to find the press room.
I remember dating a photographer who always criticized the framing of my amateur snapshots.
I think I accidentally wore mismatched shoes to a very serious press briefing.
I covered a historical society meeting that erupted into a near fistfight over a plaque placement.
I recall sitting in a deserted park at 3 AM just trying to clear my head after a rough deadline.
I remember a childhood friend named Mark, or Matt, who moved away in fifth grade without saying goodbye.
I got a speeding ticket while rushing to the scene of a breaking news story about a fire.
I was secretly relieved when a long-term relationship ended because I didn't know how to break it off myself.
I remember trying to read War and Peace on a vacation but abandoning it after fifty pages.

The shared Google Drive at the magazine was a total graveyard of poorly named files like Final_Final_Draft_v3 and massive 50-page running agendas from the weekly editorial syncs. I could never find the right background research folders for my longform pieces because half the staff categorized them by year and the other half by source name.
I think I accidentally quoted someone off the record once, and the guilt ate at me for months.
I covered a tech conference where I didn't understand a single thing being pitched to me.
I remember a particularly aggressive swan that chased me around a pond while I was trying to eat lunch.
I bought an ugly green couch at a thrift store that I stubbornly kept for eight years.
I recall finding a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk and using it to buy a completely unnecessary amount of candy.
I remember an interview with an old war veteran who cried, and I just sat there awkwardly not knowing what to do.
I think I had the chickenpox when I was eight, but it might have been measles.
I covered a local theater production of Hamlet that was so bad I almost walked out at intermission.
I accidentally dropped my phone into a storm drain while trying to hail a cab in the rain.
I remember stealing a glance at a rival paper's front page and feeling a sharp pang of professional jealousy.
I had a goldfish that lived for a shockingly long time, maybe five years, before I woke up and found it floating.

For the 2016 election post-mortem, I had to sift through hundreds of hours of raw voter audio interviews while simultaneously trying to crunch precinct-level polling spreadsheets in SPSS. Bouncing between running sentiment coding on the qualitative quotes and running regression models on the voter turnout stats was an absolute logistical nightmare.
I recall a terrifying flight with severe turbulence where I genuinely thought the plane was going down.
I think I used to have a favorite jacket that was stolen at a dive bar, but I can't picture its color anymore.
I covered a spelling bee and felt awful when a kid misspelled a word I didn't even know.
I remember a barista who always spelled my name as Owan and I never bothered to correct her.
I recall a time I got stuck in a revolving door for an embarrassing five minutes.
I think I took a pottery class to relax, but my bowls all looked like lumpy ashtrays.
I was once diagnosed with a mild heart arrhythmia which made me confront my own mortality far earlier than I wanted to.
I covered a sanitation workers' strike and the smell of the city in August is something I will never forget.
I remember an old mentor telling me my writing was lazy, which stung but ultimately made me better.
I think I left my umbrella on the subway at least ten different times during my first year in the city.
I once accidentally tipped a waitress fifty bucks because I mistook a fifty for a five in the dark.
I remember finding an old love letter in a library book and wondering who never received it.
I covered a small-town festival dedicated to garlic, and I smelled like it for a week.
I recall feeling a profound sense of emptiness after winning an award I thought would make me happy.
I think I chipped a tooth on a stale baguette but never got it fixed properly.
I remember a particularly loud thunderstorm that knocked out the power in the newsroom right before a print deadline.
I had a brief stint where I tried to become a vegetarian, but it ended at a late-night burger joint.
I recall my parents having a screaming match in the kitchen when I was young, though I don't know what it was about.
I covered an art exhibition where someone mistook me for the artist and I just played along for a few minutes.
I think my first computer was a clunky desktop that made dial-up noises that sounded like screeching cats.
I remember losing my voice completely for three days and having to conduct interviews via a notepad.
I accidentally hit a parked car in a garage and drove away without leaving a note because I panicked.
I recall taking a train across the country and spending hours staring at the endless flat landscapes.
I remember a rival journalist spreading a nasty rumor about my reporting methods that almost cost me my job.
I think I bought a bonsai tree once, but it died within a month because I forgot to water it.
I covered a local chess tournament and was amazed at how fiercely aggressive the players were.
I recall eating cereal for dinner for a straight week because I was too broke to buy groceries.
I remember a childhood bully whose name I've forgotten, but I can still picture his crooked front teeth.
I once ruined a brand new shirt by dropping a meatball sub on my lap in the car.
I covered a zoo enclosure opening and an ostrich aggressively pecked at my camera lens.
I think I had a subscription to a literary magazine I never actually read, just kept on the coffee table.
I remember attending a cousin's wedding and awkwardly sitting at a table with people I didn't know.
I got incredibly lost in a maze of cubicles at a corporate headquarters while trying to find a whistleblower.
I recall a horrible flu in my thirties that left me hallucinating about giant typewriters.
I think I found a stray kitten in an alleyway once, but I took it to a shelter because my apartment didn't allow pets.
I covered a surprisingly intense pie-eating contest at a county fair.
I remember an editor who always used red pen to cross out my adjectives, muttering about 'fluff'.
I accidentally called my high school teacher 'Mom' once and felt my face burn with embarrassment.
I recall a beautiful autumn day where I just sat on a park bench and watched leaves fall for an hour.
I think I bought a terribly overpriced gym membership that I only used twice.
I remember getting a flat tire on a bridge and having to change it while semi-trucks roared past.
I covered a story about a historical mansion that was allegedly haunted, though all I felt was cold drafts.
I had a really ugly falling out with a sibling over something trivial that we never truly resolved.
I recall slipping on a patch of ice and dropping my groceries all over the sidewalk.
I think I watched a bootleg movie on a tiny laptop screen while crammed in the middle seat of an airplane.
I remember a politician winking at me after dodging my question during a press conference.
I accidentally set off the fire alarm in my apartment building while trying to cook a steak.
I covered a hot air balloon festival and the roar of the burners was deafening.
I recall a time I was deeply in debt and avoided answering my phone for fear of collectors.
I think I had a favorite mug with a crack down the side that finally shattered in the sink.
I remember interviewing an author who gave one-word answers to every single question I asked.
I accidentally left my recorder on and caught myself singing terribly to the radio.
I recall going to a terrible modern art exhibit where there was just a pile of bricks on the floor.
I covered a marathon on a blisteringly hot day and saw multiple runners collapse at the finish line.
I think I tried to build an Ikea bookshelf without instructions and ended up with extra screws.
I remember finding a deeply upsetting diary entry from a former partner that made me question our entire relationship.
I recall standing in line for hours to buy concert tickets, only to find they sold out when I reached the front.
I got trapped in a sudden downpour without a jacket and arrived at an interview looking like a drowned rat.
I covered a local diner's closing after fifty years and the owner gave me a slice of pie on the house.
I think I used to hate mushrooms until I accidentally ate them in a risotto and realized they were okay.
I remember waking up in a cold sweat thinking I missed a print deadline, only to realize it was Saturday.
I accidentally insulted a close friend's cooking to their face because I thought they were joking about making it.
I recall watching a meteor shower from the roof of my first apartment, wrapped in a blanket.
I covered a bizarre protest where people dressed as vegetables to promote a community garden.
I think I had a pen pal in France when I was in middle school, but we stopped writing after two letters.
I remember a landlord who refused to fix my leaky sink, so I just kept a bucket under it for a year.
I recall a humiliating moment where my credit card was declined while trying to pay for a business lunch.
I accidentally shrunk my favorite wool sweater in the wash and it looked fit for a toddler.
I covered a snowstorm that shut the city down and had to sleep under my desk at the paper.
I think I saw a guy playing a saxophone on the subway who was actually incredibly talented.
I remember buying a cheap watch from a street vendor that stopped working the very next day.
I recall a deeply lonely birthday where the only text I got was an automated message from my dentist.
I accidentally spilled a glass of wine on a stranger at a gallery opening and apologized profusely.
I covered a spelling bee where a kid threw a massive tantrum on stage after misspelling 'accommodate'.
I think I used to have a fear of escalators when I was a toddler, but I grew out of it.
I remember a coworker bringing incredibly pungent fish to microwave in the breakroom every Friday.
I recall finding a bird with a broken wing on my porch, but it died before I could take it to a vet.
I accidentally deleted an important contact's phone number and had to track them down through an old email.
I covered a small-town parade where the mayor waved from the back of a vintage convertible.
I think I got terribly sunburned on a cloudy day because I assumed I didn't need sunscreen.
I remember an incredibly tense interview with a police chief who glared at me the entire time.
I was once diagnosed with a mild ulcer, probably from years of stress and terrible newsroom coffee.
I recall laughing so hard at a joke my college roommate made that I actually snorted soda out my nose.
I covered a high school science fair and was genuinely intimidated by a teenager's robotics project.
I think I tried to dye my hair dark brown in my twenties, but it ended up looking like shoe polish.
I remember getting a paper cut from a fresh stack of legal documents that stung for days.
I recall accidentally leaving my laptop charger at a hotel and having to buy an overpriced replacement at the airport.
I had a crippling bout of impostor syndrome after my first front-page byline was published.
I covered a dog surfing competition once, which was both ridiculous and surprisingly entertaining.
I think I bought a lottery ticket when the jackpot was huge, even though I know the odds are terrible.
I remember a diner waitperson who always called me 'hon' and it inexplicably made my day better.
I recall a terrible blind date where the person talked exclusively about their ex for two hours.
I accidentally backed into a garbage can at the end of my driveway and left a dent in the bumper.

I used to wish there was a searchable directory that just showed exactly who in the newsroom had deep background knowledge on the zoning board without me having to shout across the bullpen. If I could have just seen that the junior political reporter already had a cache of sources on commercial real estate, I wouldn't have spent three days cold-calling developers.
I covered an amateur wrestling match in a high school gym that smelled aggressively of bleach and sweat.
I think I lost my favorite scarf on a windy day, just watching it blow down the street out of reach.
I remember finding out a colleague was passing off my research as their own, leading to a bitter confrontation.
I recall sitting on my fire escape on a humid summer night, listening to the distant hum of city traffic.

participants.persona: Grant is a PM and Research Lead with 12 years of experience.
participants.name: Grant

memories.content: I often think about how my early obsession with organizing my childhood toys led directly to my career in product management. I guess I have always just wanted the world to follow a clear roadmap.
Looking back at my first research lead role, I realize I talked way too much during user interviews. I was so desperate to prove I knew the domain that I failed to actually listen.
I find myself wondering if my reliance on data is just a shield against making hard intuitive choices. It is easier to blame a failed launch on metrics than on my own judgment.
Sometimes I reflect on how I handled the restructure five years ago, knowing I was too cold about the layoffs. I was trying to be professional, but it just came off as robotic.
I realize now that my habit of arriving early to everything stems from my dad's constant lateness when I was a kid. I promised myself I would never make people wait the way he did.
It is strange to recognize that I enjoy the planning phase of a project far more than the execution. I think I am just in love with the idealized version of things before reality hits.
Whenever I look at old photos from college, I am struck by how desperate I was to fit in. I can see the forced smiles and realize how long it took to actually become myself.
I often evaluate my career progress against my peers, which I know is a toxic habit. I keep telling myself I am on my own path, but the insecurity still creeps in.
I look back on my twenties and realize I spent way too much time worrying about what my managers thought of me. I wish I had trusted my own research instincts earlier.
It dawned on me recently that I use humor to deflect when a product review isn't going well. It is a defense mechanism I have carried over from my awkward teenage years.
I am hyper-aware of how my tone shifts when I am presenting to stakeholders versus my internal team. I feel like an actor putting on different masks depending on the audience.
Looking at my old notebooks, I see how much my handwriting has degraded since everything went digital. It makes me wonder what other small physical skills I have slowly lost over the years.
I remember the heavy silence in the room when my first startup officially went under. I felt like a complete failure, though the exact words the CEO said are a blur now.
There was a time I cried in my car after a brutal performance review early in my career. The feeling of utter inadequacy was suffocating, even if I don't remember all the specific feedback.
I can still feel the panic of the afternoon I realized I had accidentally deleted an entire week of raw user research data. My stomach completely dropped, and I felt sick for days.
I remember the exact smell of the hospital waiting room when my brother was in surgery. The sheer terror of sitting in those stiff chairs is something I will never forget.
I recall the deep shame I felt when a senior PM caught me lying about having finished a competitor analysis. I stumbled over my words and just wanted the floor to swallow me.
The day my long-term partner and I split up, I remember the cold draft in the apartment. I felt entirely hollowed out, unable to process what my future would look like.
I still get anxious thinking about the time I had a full panic attack before a major keynote presentation. My chest was so tight I thought I was having a heart attack.
I remember the quiet devastation of reading the email that my close mentor had unexpectedly passed away. The office around me just kept moving, but I felt entirely paralyzed.
I can recall the bitter taste of cheap wine from the nights I used to drink alone in my early twenties just to fall asleep. It was a dark period of my life that I rarely talk about.
I remember the acute embarrassment of my credit card being declined at a team dinner when I was still an unpaid intern. I could feel my face burning as someone else quietly picked up the tab.
I vividly remember the smell of fresh whiteboard markers when we kicked off the new app redesign. The excitement in the room was palpable, though I forget who actually led the session.
I remember walking through a park in Seattle during a work trip and being amazed by the massive pine trees. The air felt incredibly crisp and clean.
There was this one coffee shop near my first apartment that played loud jazz music every Sunday morning. I loved the energy, even if the coffee itself was always burnt.
I recall a user testing session where the participant kept clicking the logo instead of the home button. It was incredibly frustrating to watch, though I can't picture their face anymore.
I remember the warmth of the sun on my back during a childhood family trip to the beach. We spent hours building sandcastles that the tide eventually washed away.
I once spent an entire weekend assembling a ridiculous piece of IKEA furniture. I just remember the sore fingers and the vague triumph when it finally stood upright.
The taste of my grandmother's lemon cake is something I can still almost conjure up. It was perfectly tart, though I don't think anyone ever wrote down the recipe.
I remember sitting on the floor of my dorm room, eating cold noodles and studying for a psychology exam. The room was terribly drafty in the winter.
I recall the sheer relief of finally submitting a massive research report after pulling a near all-nighter. I slept for twelve hours straight right after.
I remember a road trip with friends where we got completely lost in the mountains because we had no cell service. The stars were unbelievably bright that night.

I remember being incredibly frustrated during the Q3 planning cycle because I needed to know who on the backend team had context on the old billing API, but I hated having to spam the Slack channel just to find the right person. If we just had a passive directory of who owns what knowledge, I wouldn't have wasted days waiting for async replies.
There was a dog in my neighborhood growing up that would always bark at bicycles. I remember the rattling sound of the chain-link fence as it jumped up.
I remember the satisfying click of closing my laptop after my very first successful product launch. The whole team went out for drinks, though I forget which bar we went to.
I recall watching a thunderstorm roll in from the balcony of my old apartment. The sudden drop in temperature before the rain hit was always my favorite part.
I once had a manager who always used the phrase circle back in every single meeting. It became a running joke among the research team.
I remember the sharp smell of chlorine from early morning swim practices in high school. The water was always freezing when I first jumped in.
I have a vague memory of a street musician playing a saxophone in the subway station on my commute. The melody was hauntingly beautiful, but I only heard it that one time.
I remember a team offsite where we had to do a trust fall exercise, and I was terrified the person behind me wouldn't catch me. They did, but my heart was pounding.
I recall the frustration of my first car constantly overheating in summer traffic. I spent a lot of time sitting on the side of the highway waiting for it to cool down.
I remember the vibrant orange color of the fall leaves during my first semester of college. The campus looked like a postcard for a few fleeting weeks.
There was an old diner we used to go to after late-night study sessions that served the best greasy hash browns. I remember the cracked red vinyl booths clearly.
I recall a particularly tense sprint planning meeting where two engineers started shouting at each other. The tension in the air was thick, but I don't remember what the feature was.
I remember the quiet hum of the servers in the IT closet at my first corporate job. It was oddly peaceful to hide in there for a few minutes when the office got too loud.
I can still feel the texture of the rough carpet in my childhood bedroom. I used to lie on it for hours reading comic books.
I remember a beautiful sunset on a flight back from Tokyo, the clouds lit up in neon pinks and purples. I pressed my forehead against the cold window to watch it.
I recall the annoyance of dealing with a perfectly good umbrella that flipped inside out during a sudden rainstorm. I ended up just throwing it in a public trash can.
There was a user interview once where the person's cat kept walking across their keyboard. It was distracting but gave us all a good laugh.
I remember the intense smell of garlic in the hallway of my first apartment building. It always made me hungry right as I was getting home from work.
I recall the excitement of buying my first professional suit for an interview. It felt a little too stiff, but I walked out of the store feeling like a real adult.
I remember watching a documentary about deep-sea creatures that kept me awake half the night. The glowing jellyfish were mesmerising.
I recall dropping my phone on a concrete sidewalk and the agonizing second before I flipped it over to check the screen. It was totally shattered.
I remember a coworker bringing in homemade tamales for the whole office during the holidays. The masa was perfectly soft and savory.
I have a memory of walking barefoot on wet grass after a summer barbecue. The coolness felt amazing against my feet.
I recall a brainstorming session where the whiteboard was completely filled with sticky notes of every color. The visual chaos was weirdly inspiring.
I remember the distinctive sound of my grandfather's old grandfather clock ticking in the hallway. It was a slow, heavy sound that echoed in the quiet house.
I once tried to learn how to play the guitar but gave up after a few weeks. I just remember how much my fingertips hurt from the strings.
I recall the intense relief of stepping into an air-conditioned movie theater on a sweltering July afternoon. The blast of cold air was instantly reviving.
I remember a stray cat that used to hang around our office parking lot. Someone eventually adopted it, but I still remember its loud meows.
I can still picture the confusing layout of the grocery store in my old neighborhood. I could never find the cereal aisle on the first try.
I remember the taste of the slightly stale popcorn I ate at a drive-in movie theater. The movie itself is completely gone from my memory.
I recall the satisfying feeling of peeling the protective plastic off a brand-new monitor. It was the best part of getting upgraded equipment at work.
I remember a terribly bumpy ferry ride where almost everyone on board got seasick. I just gripped the railing and stared at the horizon the whole time.
I have a memory of a childhood friend's basement that always smelled like damp cardboard. We used to play video games down there for hours.
I recall the quiet focus of a library during finals week, with everyone hunched over their laptops. The silence was heavy and productive.
I remember the sudden, loud crack of thunder that once woke me up in the middle of the night. It shook the entire house.
I once bought a wildly expensive coffee machine that took me a week to figure out. The first cup I made was incredibly bitter.
I recall a time I accidentally boarded the wrong train and ended up in a suburb I didn't recognize. The panic was brief but intense before I found my way back.

Searching Confluence for the European market research last year was infuriating because I didn't know the legacy growth team always tagged those files under the Project Griffin codename. Keyword search is completely useless if you don't already know the exact obscure terminology the original authors used.
I remember the bright, flashing lights of an arcade I went to for a friend's birthday party. The noise of all the games blending together was deafening.
I can still taste the incredibly spicy salsa from a tiny taqueria near my college campus. My eyes watered every time, but I couldn't stop eating it.
I remember the satisfying weight of the first real trophy I won in a youth soccer league. It sat on my bookshelf for over a decade.
I recall watching a street artist spray-paint a massive mural on a brick wall. The smell of the paint was overwhelming, but the art was incredible.
I remember the frustration of a software crash right before I saved a massive strategy document. I just sat at my desk and stared at the frozen screen.
I have a memory of flying a kite at a windy park when I was young. The pull of the string in my hand felt surprisingly strong.
I recall a really awkward elevator ride with the company CEO where neither of us said a word. The silence stretched on forever.
I remember the comforting warmth of a heavy winter coat the first time I wore it in the snow. It felt like walking around in a sleeping bag.
I once attended a terribly boring conference panel where half the audience was checking their phones. The fluorescent lights overhead gave me a headache.
I recall the crunch of autumn leaves under my boots during a hike in the woods. The air smelled earthy and crisp.
I remember a street festival where I ate a massive, overly sweet funnel cake. My hands were sticky with powdered sugar for the rest of the day.
I can still hear the rhythmic thumping of the bass from a concert I attended in my twenties. My ears rang for a full day afterward.
I remember the sheer panic of misplacing my passport at the airport right before a flight. I found it in my jacket pocket, but my heart was racing.
I recall a massive snowstorm that shut down the city for two days. The quietness of the empty streets was eerie and beautiful.
I remember the distinct smell of old, dusty books in the back corner of a used bookstore. I used to spend rainy afternoons just browsing the shelves.
I have a vague memory of a primary school teacher who always wore bright yellow dresses. She had a very loud, booming laugh.
I recall the strange sensation of zero gravity during a VR simulation we tested for work. It genuinely made my stomach drop for a second.
I remember burning my tongue on a slice of pizza that was fresh out of the oven. The cheese blistered the roof of my mouth.
I once found a perfectly intact bird's nest in the bushes outside my house. I was amazed by how intricately the twigs were woven together.
I recall a chaotic morning where I spilled coffee all over my shirt just before a client meeting. I had to wear my coat indoors for the entire pitch.
I remember the soothing sound of waves crashing against the rocks during a beach vacation. It put me to sleep every night.
I can still picture the terrible neon green paint in the bathroom of my first rental house. It was incredibly jarring every time I turned on the light.
I remember the excitement of finding a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk when I was a teenager. I felt rich for the entire afternoon.
I recall the smell of roasted peanuts at a baseball game I went to with my dad. The stadium lights were blindingly bright.
I remember a particularly grueling flight delay where I sat at the gate for six hours. The uncomfortable airport chairs made my back ache for days.
I have a memory of a thunderstorm so bad it knocked out the power in our neighborhood. We spent the evening playing board games by candlelight.
I recall the sharp scent of pine needles from a real Christmas tree we had one year. It made the whole house smell like a forest.
I remember the anxiety of parallel parking on a busy street during my driving test. My hands were sweating profusely on the steering wheel.
I once saw a double rainbow after a heavy spring shower and just stood on my porch staring at it. The colors were incredibly vivid against the grey sky.
I recall a time I tried to cook a fancy dinner and completely burned the main course. We ended up ordering takeout instead.
I remember the chaotic energy of the trading floor when I visited a finance client. The shouting and rapid movements were totally overwhelming.
I can still feel the icy blast of winter wind hitting my face as I walked to the subway. It felt like tiny needles on my skin.

I still get a headache thinking about how differently we had to structure our product roadmap in Jira compared to managing the raw qualitative transcripts in Dovetail. A rigid taxonomy works perfectly for engineering tickets, but it completely falls apart when you're trying to synthesize messy, open-ended user interview data.
I remember the satisfaction of clearing out my email inbox before leaving for a long vacation. It felt like a massive weight had been lifted.
I recall a childhood pet hamster that used to run on its squeaky wheel all night long. It was annoying, but I missed the sound when it was gone.
I remember the thrill of riding a massive roller coaster that went upside down. The initial drop left my stomach in the air.

When we first migrated the UX research hub to Notion, I loved the blank canvas, but within a month Sarah and the other PMs had built so many nested databases that no one knew where to put anything. The flexibility was amazing at first, but the sheer feature bloat ended up paralyzing the junior researchers.
I have a memory of a coworker's desk that was absolutely covered in small action figures. It was a nightmare to dust, I imagine.
I recall the sweet taste of fresh strawberries picked right from the garden. They were warm from the afternoon sun.
I remember the exhaustion of packing moving boxes until three in the morning. My arms felt like lead the next day.
I once took a pottery class and found the feeling of wet clay on the wheel surprisingly therapeutic. My bowl turned out terribly lopsided, though.
I recall a sudden downpour that caught me without an umbrella on my lunch break. I arrived back at the office completely drenched.
I remember the distinct mechanical hum of an old refrigerator in my college dorm. It always kicked on just as I was trying to fall asleep.
I can still picture the intricate frost patterns on my windowpane during a deep winter freeze. They looked like delicate crystal ferns.
I remember the pride of finally finishing a dense, thousand-page novel I had been reading for months. I closed the cover with a satisfying thud.
I recall a time I accidentally used salt instead of sugar in my morning coffee. The first sip was an absolute shock to the system.
I remember the vibrant, chaotic atmosphere of a night market I visited in Taiwan. The smell of stinky tofu permeated the humid air.
I have a memory of a badly organized hackathon where no one slept for forty-eight hours. We survived purely on pizza and energy drinks.
I recall the gentle rocking motion of a hammock I lay in during a summer retreat. The dappled sunlight through the trees was mesmerizing.
I remember the annoyance of getting a flat tire on a deserted stretch of highway. Changing it in the dark was a frustrating experience.

I will never forget the relief I felt when we piloted that AI search tool that could instantly pull up a three-bullet summary of a forty-page product spec. As a PM juggling five different feature squads, I don't have time to dig through dense documentation and desperately need smart indexing to give me a rapid snapshot of the core constraints.
I once found an old, faded photograph tucked inside a secondhand book I bought. It was of a family smiling on a beach, and I always wondered who they were.
I recall the sharp tang of a blood orange I ate for breakfast one morning. The color of the juice was surprisingly dark.
I remember the booming voice of a theater director from a college play I did sound design for. He commanded the room without even trying.
I can still feel the coarse sand between my toes from a late-night walk along the shoreline. The water was surprisingly warm.
I remember a terribly awkward team-building exercise where we had to maintain eye contact for a full minute. I kept wanting to burst out laughing.
I recall the smell of damp earth in a greenhouse filled with exotic orchids. The humidity was thick and heavy on my skin.
I remember a time I tried to assemble a complicated tent in the dark while camping. I ended up just sleeping in the car out of frustration.
I have a memory of a local bakery that always sold out of croissants by eight in the morning. The buttery smell lingered on the street all day.
I recall the deep, resonant sound of a cello being played by a street busker. It made me stop in my tracks and listen for a while.
I remember the dizzying heights from the observation deck of a skyscraper in Chicago. The cars below looked like tiny crawling insects.
I once spilled a glass of red wine on a friend's white rug and felt incredibly guilty. We scrubbed at it for an hour, but the stain stayed.
I recall the strange, metallic taste of tap water in a city I was visiting for a conference. I had to buy bottled water for the rest of the trip.
I remember the intense concentration of watching a progress bar slowly creep to 100 percent on a major software update. I was holding my breath at the very end.
I can still picture the bright yellow rain boots I insisted on wearing every day as a kid. They were a size too big and clunked when I walked.
I remember the comforting smell of woodsmoke from a chimney on a crisp autumn evening. It instantly made me want to sit by a fire.
I recall a time my alarm didn't go off and I woke up entirely disoriented an hour late. The rush to get out the door was chaotic.
I remember a beautiful, intricately carved wooden door on an old church I passed during a walk. I ran my fingers over the deep grooves in the wood.
I have a vague memory of my mother's perfume, which smelled strongly of jasmine and rose. It always lingered in the hallway after she left for work.
I recall the frustration of dealing with a tangled ball of fairy lights right before the holidays. It took me hours of meticulous work to unravel them.
I remember the jarring sound of a fire alarm going off in the middle of a serious strategy meeting. We all had to stand awkwardly in the parking lot for twenty minutes.
I once dropped a freshly made sandwich right on the kitchen floor. The disappointment was strangely disproportionate to the event.
I recall the dazzling brightness of fresh snow on a sunny winter morning. I had to squint just to look out the window.
I remember a cramped, dusty antique shop where I found a beautiful old pocket watch. The ticking sound was incredibly loud in the quiet store.
I can still feel the sticky humidity of a July afternoon in Washington DC. The air felt heavy enough to swim in.

The churn analysis presentation last winter was a mess because I hadn't realized the marketing folks had already tried and abandoned a similar retention strategy two years prior. Without shared historical context in our systems, it is virtually impossible to know who the real cross-functional stakeholders are before you step on a political landmine.
I remember the satisfying snap of breaking a fresh piece of chocolate off the bar. It was a dark chocolate with sea salt, my favorite.
I recall a time I got caught in a revolving door with someone who was walking too slowly. It was a brief, awkward shuffle to get out.
I remember the mesmerizing pattern of a kaleidoscope I played with as a child. The shifting colors seemed completely magical to me then.
I have a memory of a coworker who clicked their pen incessantly during every meeting. It drove me absolutely crazy, though I never said anything.
I recall the comforting heaviness of a weighted blanket I bought during a stressful work phase. It helped me sleep through the night for the first time in weeks.
I remember a stray dog that followed me for three blocks before wandering off. It had bright, intelligent eyes that stuck in my memory.
I once tried to fix a leaky sink myself and ended up soaking the entire bathroom floor. I had to call a plumber the very next morning.
I recall the sharp, acidic taste of a bad cup of espresso at a rest stop. It was hot enough to burn, but terrible to drink.
I remember the awe of seeing the Milky Way for the first time in a dark sky preserve. The sheer number of stars was staggering.
I can still picture the scuffed tips of my favorite pair of leather boots. I wore them until the soles practically fell off.
I remember the rhythmic sound of a train rolling over the tracks during a cross-country trip. It was oddly hypnotic and lulled me to sleep.
I recall a time I completely forgot the name of a key stakeholder during a presentation. The blank space in my brain was terrifying, but I managed to gloss over it.
I remember the smell of fresh paint in my first real office. It gave me a slight headache, but I was too proud of the promotion to care.
I have a memory of a massive spider web stretching across my front porch one autumn morning. The morning dew made it sparkle in the light.
I recall the satisfying sound of scissors gliding through a piece of wrapping paper without tearing it. It is a tiny perfection that always feels good.
I remember a crowded subway car where someone was playing a loud accordion. It was annoying, but undeniably festive.
I once watched a pigeon confidently walk onto a bus and ride it for two stops. It was the most bizarre, mundane thing I have ever seen.
I recall the intense burn of muscle soreness two days after starting a new workout routine. Walking down the stairs was sheer agony.
I remember a terrible haircut I got right before starting a new job. I spent a month trying to style it differently every day to hide the mistake.
I can still smell the mix of old paper and dust in the university archives. I spent hours down there researching for my thesis.
I remember the comforting sound of rain hitting the tin roof of a cabin I rented. It was the perfect background noise for reading.
I recall a time I accidentally sent an email to the entire company instead of one person. The immediate panic was a horrible feeling, though the email was harmless.
I remember the sweet, rich taste of maple syrup on fresh pancakes at a diner in Vermont. The butter melted perfectly over the stack.
I have a vague memory of a clown at a birthday party who absolutely terrified me as a child. I hid behind a couch for the entire performance.
I recall the frustration of trying to peel a hard-boiled egg where the shell stuck to the egg white. It ended up looking like a mangled mess.
I remember the sharp sting of a paper cut from a fresh manila folder. It throbbed annoyingly for the rest of the day.
I once attended a wedding where the groom completely forgot his vows and just improvised. It was hilarious and incredibly endearing.
I recall the smell of ozone right before a massive summer thunderstorm hit the city. The sky turned an eerie, bruised shade of green.
I remember the intense concentration required to balance a wobbly table at a restaurant with folded coasters. It became a mini-mission before the food arrived.
I can still picture the intricate, colorful patterns on a rug my parents brought back from a trip. I used to trace the shapes with my finger.
I remember a terribly turbulent flight where the overhead bins rattled violently. I gripped the armrests so hard my knuckles turned white.
I recall the satisfying thwack of hitting a tennis ball right in the sweet spot of the racket. It felt effortless and powerful.
I remember a time I tried to bake bread from scratch and ended up with a brick of dough. I severely underestimated how much yeast mattered.
I have a memory of a streetlamp outside my old apartment that would flicker incessantly. It drove me crazy until the city finally fixed it.
I recall the sweet smell of honeysuckle bushes that lined the fence of my childhood backyard. The scent was incredibly strong in the late afternoons.
I remember the anxiety of watching my battery drop to one percent while I was navigating an unfamiliar city. The phone died right as I found my hotel.
I once stood in line for three hours just to try a famous pastry, and it was decidedly mediocre. The anticipation was much better than the actual food.
I recall the sound of crunching gravel under the tires as we pulled into my grandparents' driveway. It always signaled the start of a long holiday weekend.
I remember a particularly intense game of chess I played with a colleague during a long layover. We were both surprisingly competitive about it.
I can still feel the harsh glare of the fluorescent lights in a twenty-four-hour laundromat I used to frequent. The hum of the dryers was constant.
I remember the sudden, freezing shock of jumping into a lake in early June. The water hadn't warmed up at all from the winter.
I recall the distinctive smell of permanent markers from a whiteboarding session that went on for six hours. The room was poorly ventilated.
I remember a time I found a perfectly preserved autumn leaf pressed inside a library book. It was a small, beautiful surprise.
I have a vague memory of my first bicycle, which had brightly colored streamers on the handlebars. I thought it made me go faster.
I recall the intense, spicy aroma of a curry dish cooking in the apartment down the hall. It always made me want to order takeout.
I remember the frustration of dropping a tiny screw while assembling a desk and never finding it. The desk is still missing that one piece to this day.
I once got caught in a sudden hailstorm and had to seek shelter under a bridge. The sound of the hail hitting the concrete was deafening.
I recall the warm, soft texture of a cashmere sweater I splurged on with my first real bonus. It felt incredibly luxurious.
I remember a terrible sunburn I got on my shoulders after forgetting to reapply sunscreen at a company picnic. The peeling phase was awful.
I can still picture the exact shade of teal of a vintage typewriter I saw at a flea market but didn't buy. I have regretted leaving it behind ever since.
I remember the satisfying weight of an old, heavy ceramic coffee mug I used to keep on my desk. It kept my coffee warm for hours.
I recall the sharp chirp of a cricket that somehow got into my bedroom and kept me awake. I searched for an hour but never found it.
I remember the blinding reflection of the sun off a glass skyscraper while I was walking to lunch. I had to shield my eyes the entire block.
I have a memory of trying to fold a massive fitted sheet and eventually just rolling it into a messy ball. I always convince myself I will learn how to do it properly next time.

participants.persona: Elena is a Startup Founder with 9 years of experience.
participants.name: Elena

memories.content: I remember the smell of wet wool from my winter coat after playing in the Chicago snow.
My sister Clara and I used to build massive forts out of the couch cushions on Sunday mornings.
I once accidentally broke my mother's favorite vase and blamed it on the dog.
My dad missed my high school graduation because he was on a bender.
I can still taste the overly sweet cherry popsicles we bought from the ice cream truck down the street.
I realize now that my obsession with organizing my childhood desk was the first sign of my entrepreneurial need for control.
During third grade, I won the spelling bee by correctly spelling the word 'chrysanthemum'.
I used to hide under my bed with a flashlight to read mystery novels long after my bedtime.
My grandmother taught me how to make fresh pasta on her cramped kitchen counter.
I remember crying uncontrollably when my pet goldfish died, burying it ceremoniously in the backyard.
In middle school, I wore terrible blue eyeshadow because I thought it made me look mature.
I shoplifted a lipstick when I was fourteen, and the shame still haunts me whenever I enter a pharmacy.
My first job was scooping ice cream at a local parlor during the blistering summer of my sophomore year.

When scaling our engineering team last year, I constantly wished for a dashboard that indexed what specific APIs or legacy codebases developers like Marcus had mastered, rather than having to ping them on Slack every time we scoped a new feature.
I failed my first driving test because I parallel parked entirely on the sidewalk.
Getting my acceptance letter to the University of Michigan was one of the happiest days of my teenage life.
I used to sneak out of the house to meet up with friends at a 24-hour diner.
My high school biology teacher, Mr. Harrison, was the first person to tell me I was a natural leader.
I sprained my ankle severely during a varsity soccer game and had to wear a boot for two months.
I remember the exact mixtape I played on a loop during my first major breakup.
Looking back at my college essays, I can see how desperate I was to prove my intelligence to my parents.
Moving into my college dorm in Ann Arbor was chaotic, with boxes piled to the ceiling.
I survived my freshman year entirely on cheap ramen and dining hall pizza.
My roommate and I stayed up until 4 AM arguing about philosophy before our midterm exam.
I had an abortion when I was twenty-two because I knew I wasn't ready to be a mother.
Walking across the Diag in the freezing winter wind made me question my college choice every January.
I joined a business fraternity mostly because I wanted access to their test banks.
I once spilled hot coffee all over my laptop during a finals week cram session in the library.
My favorite college memory is jumping into the campus fountain fully clothed after finishing my last exam.
I took a pottery class as an elective and made a lopsided mug that I still use today.
I worked as a teaching assistant for an intro economics class and loved grading the terrible essays.
Graduating magna cum laude felt like a relief rather than a celebration.
I packed everything I owned into a rented sedan and drove across the country to San Francisco.
My first apartment in the city was a tiny studio with a window that faced a brick wall.
I spent my first year in corporate consulting making overly complex spreadsheets that nobody ever read.
My first startup attempt failed so badly that I had to move back into my childhood bedroom at twenty-five.
I met my co-founder Marcus at a dreary networking event in a hotel lobby.
We sketched out the initial idea for our company on the back of a cocktail napkin.
Quitting my stable corporate job to start the company felt like jumping off a cliff.
I maxed out three credit cards to make payroll in our second year, hiding the debt from my family.
Sometimes I wonder if I chose to build a startup just to avoid having to answer to a traditional boss.
Our first office was a converted garage that smelled faintly of motor oil and old pizza.
I remember the absolute thrill of getting our very first paying customer notification.
We used to work fourteen-hour days, surviving on endless cups of burnt drip coffee.
I accidentally deleted our entire production database during our beta launch and panicked for hours.
Marcus and I once got into a screaming match over the color of our logo's font.
I had a severe panic attack before our Series A pitch and had to hide in a stairwell.
Signing the term sheet for our first major funding round felt entirely surreal.
We bought a cheap disco ball and turned it on every time we closed a new enterprise deal.
Firing my first employee made me throw up in the office bathroom beforehand.
I often think about how my definition of success has shifted from pure wealth to simply having agency over my time.
Moving into our real office space with glass walls made us feel like a legitimate business.
I bought myself a vintage leather jacket with my first actual founder salary paycheck.
Our platform crashed on Thanksgiving Day, and the engineering team had to fix it while eating turkey.
I flew to London for a conference and ended up getting massive food poisoning at the hotel.
We instituted a dog-friendly office policy mostly so I could bring in my new puppy, Barnaby.
Getting sued by our first competitor kept me awake for three weeks straight.
I learned how to negotiate by reading bargaining books on the subway commute.
My parents finally understood what my company did when we were featured in a major tech magazine.
I accidentally called an investor 'Mom' at the end of a very long Zoom call.
It scares me to realize that my entire sense of self-worth is tied to my company's month-over-month growth.
I adopted Barnaby from a local shelter because he was the only dog not barking at me.
Barnaby completely chewed through my favorite pair of running shoes during his teething phase.
Taking the dog for a walk at 6 AM has become the most peaceful part of my daily routine.
I once lost Barnaby at the dog park for ten minutes and experienced pure terror.
He has a very specific spot on the couch where he sleeps while I answer emails.
I taught him how to high-five, which remains my proudest non-professional achievement.
We went camping in Big Sur, and Barnaby tried to chase a raccoon up a redwood tree.
I buy him unnecessarily expensive organic dog treats because I am a typical millennial pet owner.
When I look at Barnaby, I realize he is the only creature in my life that doesn't expect me to be productive.
My dog absolutely hates the mail carrier and will bark at the door for ten minutes after he leaves.
I started rock climbing five years ago as a way to force my brain to stop thinking about work.
The first time I completed a 5.10 route, my hands were bleeding, but I felt invincible.
I bought a chalk bag with a cartoon monster on it because it makes me smile.
I fell off a bouldering wall awkwardly and sprained my wrist right before a major board meeting.
My climbing partner, Sarah, is the most aggressively optimistic person I have ever met.
We took a climbing trip to Joshua Tree and slept in the back of my SUV.
I love the rough, calloused texture my hands have developed from years of grabbing resin holds.
Climbing outdoors requires a level of trust in my gear that I struggle to extend to people.
I dropped my favorite carabiner off a cliff in Yosemite and watched it bounce into the void.
I've noticed that I use humor as a defense mechanism whenever board meetings get too tense.
Cooking elaborate Sunday dinners is my favorite way to prepare for the upcoming work week.
I spent an entire weekend perfecting a recipe for homemade sourdough bread during the pandemic.
My attempt at making beef wellington for a dinner party ended in a soggy, unedible disaster.
I absolutely despise chopping onions because my eyes water excessively, no matter what tricks I try.
The farmers market at the Ferry Building is my weekend sanctuary, despite the crowds.
I buy fresh eucalyptus every week to hang in my shower because it smells like a spa.
I once set the smoke alarm off while trying to sear steaks, and the entire apartment complex was evacuated.
My grandmother's cast-iron skillet is the most valuable thing I own in my kitchen.
I have a terrible habit of eating cold leftovers straight out of the fridge at midnight.
Reflecting on my last relationship, I recognize that I was the one who pulled away first out of fear of commitment.
My last relationship ended because we couldn't agree on whether to stay in the city or move to the suburbs.
I once went on a blind date where the guy talked exclusively about his cryptocurrency portfolio.

During our Series A sprint, my product managers were slinging user research findings and market analyses across Slack, Notion, and email, completely lacking a unified taxonomy for how to store or archive those insights.
I find dating apps exhausting and usually delete them after three days of swiping.
My ex-boyfriend used to leave wet towels on the bed, which drove me absolutely insane.
I still have a shoebox of letters from my first high school boyfriend hidden in my closet.
We spent our anniversary in Paris, but it poured rain the entire time, so we just ate cheese in the hotel.
I caught my partner of three years lying about his finances, which instantly shattered my trust.
Being single in my thirties feels empowering most days, but deeply lonely on Sunday afternoons.
I once dated a chef who made me the most incredible late-night meals after his shift.
I catch myself judging people who work nine-to-five jobs, which is a toxic habit I need to unlearn.
San Francisco fog rolling over the hills is a sight that still takes my breath away.
I had my car broken into three times in one year, so now I leave the windows rolled down.
The steep hill I have to walk up to get to my apartment is my daily unwanted cardio workout.
I know the barista at my local coffee shop so well that she starts making my oat milk latte when I walk in.
I love walking through Golden Gate Park on misty mornings when the paths are empty.
The first minor earthquake I felt terrified me, but now I barely look up from my laptop.

I explicitly told our operations lead, Sarah, that any AI tool we adopt needs to output quarterly OKR reports in our exact custom Google Sheets template. Otherwise, the leadership team spends hours reformatting the raw data before board meetings.
I have a favorite spot at Ocean Beach where I go to scream at the waves when I'm stressed.
Taking the cable car feels like a tourist trap, but I secretly love doing it when family visits.
I once found a perfectly good mid-century modern chair abandoned on the sidewalk and dragged it home.
It took me years to understand that my mother's harsh criticism was actually just her own internalized anxiety.
I visited Japan for two weeks and ate nothing but convenience store egg sandwiches and incredible ramen.
The neon lights in Tokyo gave me a sensory overload, but in the best way possible.
I got terribly lost in Kyoto because my phone died, but ended up discovering a hidden shrine.
We took a company retreat to Lake Tahoe, and half the team got sunburned while kayaking.
I learned how to ski as an adult and spent three days entirely on the bunny hill.
My flight to New York was delayed by twelve hours, so I slept on the airport floor using my backpack as a pillow.
I hate packing so much that I usually just throw random clothes into a suitcase hours before a flight.
In Italy, I drank so much espresso that my hands literally shook during a museum tour.
I collect ugly refrigerator magnets from every city I visit as a private joke with myself.
I am acutely aware that my public persona as a 'confident founder' is mostly just well-rehearsed acting.
I love the feeling of freshly washed sheets right after taking a hot shower.
My sister and I didn't speak for a year after a fight over our grandmother's estate.
Clara finally called me on my birthday to apologize, and we both cried on the phone.
I send my parents a bouquet of flowers every anniversary because I know they won't celebrate otherwise.
Whenever I go back to Chicago, the freezing wind hits my face and instantly reminds me of my childhood.
I helped my dad fix the back deck last summer, and we actually managed not to argue.
I absolutely hate the sound of people chewing loudly, to the point where I have to leave the room.
I have a scar on my left knee from tripping over a sprinkler head when I was nine.
I drink exactly one glass of red wine every Thursday night while watching trashy reality television.
I sometimes reflect on the fact that I haven't made a completely new friend outside of the tech industry in five years.
My favorite book is a beat-up copy of 'Dune' that I've read at least seven times.

After a major customer churn event in 2021, the customer success team compiled a brilliant post-mortem but couldn't figure out who in the backend infrastructure team actually needed to see the latency findings.
I went through a phase where I exclusively listened to true crime podcasts, which gave me terrible nightmares.
I always kill my houseplants, no matter how much attention I give them.
I lost my temper and screamed at Marcus in front of the whole engineering team, which I deeply regret.
We had to hire an executive coach to help fix the communication breakdown between the founders.

Our shared Google Drive became an absolute nightmare by year three, filled with vaguely named files like Final_Pitch_Deck_v4 and massive, unnavigable fifty-page running meeting agendas that nobody could parse.
I once locked my keys inside my apartment and had to pay a locksmith three hundred dollars to let me in.
I am convinced that my phone listens to my conversations to serve me targeted ads.
I have an irrational fear of crossing metal grate bridges while driving.
I buy a new physical planner every January and completely abandon it by March.
Looking at my packed calendar, I realize I use busyness to avoid sitting alone with my thoughts.
My favorite piece of clothing is a massive, incredibly ugly wool sweater I bought at a thrift store.
I used to play the flute in middle school, but I was aggressively terrible at it.
I love the smell of gasoline at gas stations, even though I know it's toxic.
I accidentally dyed my hair jet black in college when I was aiming for dark brown.
I once found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk and spent it immediately on an overpriced lunch.
A bird pooped on my head on my way to a crucial pitch meeting.
I love thunderstorms, mostly because we don't get many of them in California.
My first car was a rusty Honda Civic that vibrated violently if I drove over sixty miles an hour.
I backed that Honda Civic into a light pole two days after getting my license.
I recognize now that my impatience with my employees stems directly from my own imposter syndrome.
I bought a fancy road bike but mostly just use it to ride slowly along the Embarcadero.
I can't sleep unless I have a fan running for background noise.
I ate nothing but saltines for two days when I caught the flu last winter.
I once completely forgot my own phone number when filling out a medical form.
I have a weird habit of counting the stairs whenever I walk up a flight.
I despise wearing high heels and exclusively wear sneakers to formal tech events.
My favorite movie is an obscure 90s rom-com that I refuse to admit I like.
I cry during commercials featuring dogs, without fail.
I accidentally sent a venting text about a client to that exact client, which cost us the account.
I was bullied in fifth grade for having frizzy hair, and I still straighten it obsessively today.
I have a recurring dream where I am back in college and haven't attended a single math class.
I bought a hammock for my balcony, but the sun glares directly into my eyes whenever I use it.
I used to collect vintage stamps when I was younger, keeping them in a pristine leather binder.
I absolutely love spicy food, but it always gives me terrible heartburn later.
I once tried to build a custom mechanical keyboard and gave up after ruining three switches.
My dog hates the vacuum cleaner and tries to bite it every time I turn it on.
I went to a music festival in the desert and hated the dust so much I left a day early.
I am fiercely competitive at board games, which makes me very annoying to play Catan with.
I won a pumpkin carving contest in our neighborhood by making a perfect replica of the Mona Lisa.
I once spent an hour arguing with Marcus about the exact shade of blue for our checkout button.
I signed up for a half marathon and only trained for three weeks beforehand, which was agonizing.
I love the quiet hum of a server room, even though I rarely need to go into them anymore.
I once ate an entire pint of ice cream after a bad date and felt zero regrets.
I have an uncanny ability to guess exactly what time it is without looking at a clock.
I keep a jar of emergency peanut butter in my office desk drawer.
I got a parking ticket yesterday because I misread the impossibly confusing street signs.
I watched a documentary about deep-sea creatures and felt slightly terrified of the ocean for weeks.
I have a subscription to a fancy print magazine that I never actually read, but I like how it looks on my coffee table.
I accidentally superglued my fingers together while trying to fix a broken coffee mug.
I survived my twenties on shockingly little sleep and copious amounts of cheap diner coffee.
My parents recently mentioned downsizing their house, which gave me an unexpected wave of sadness.
I bought my mom a beautiful silk scarf from Italy, but she insists on saving it for 'special occasions' that never happen.
I found a gray hair this morning and immediately plucked it out with tweezers.
I have a bad habit of biting my nails whenever I review legal contracts.
I took a spontaneous road trip up Highway 1 and pulled over just to watch the sunset over the Pacific.
I once convinced a bouncer I was on the guest list of a club just by acting incredibly annoyed.
I hate automated customer service phone lines and will press zero repeatedly to talk to a human.
I love the crisp smell of new books, so I refuse to buy a digital e-reader.
I got trapped in an elevator for twenty minutes and ended up chatting pleasantly with a complete stranger.

I audited my own calendar last month and realized I was burning at least ten hours a week just manually adjusting permissions on Confluence pages, tagging reviewers, and hunting down sign-offs for partner agreements.
Knowing that my employees rely on me to pay their rent is a crushing weight I carry every single day.
I recently threw away out a box of old business cards from my first job, finally letting go of that past life.
I watched a pigeon steal a croissant from a cafe table today, and it was the funniest thing I've seen all week.
I spent twenty minutes looking for my sunglasses before realizing they were on top of my head.
